The second phase, a rebuild of the enclosure itself, would have to wait for the donor pledges to subside into actual deposits.

A columnist for the city paper, hostile on principle to any expenditure on zoos, called the plan groundless. He altercated, in successive Sunday columns, that money for animals should not be released while shelters for the unhoused were being closed elsewhere in the county. The argument was less convincing than its tone suggested. The director, in a public response that did not stymie the columnist but did, at least, puncture his sharper claims, pointed out that the renovation was funded by a restricted bequest that could not, by the terms of the will, have been redirected.

What captivated visitors, six months later, was something none of them could have anticipated. The tiger, given access to a deeper outdoor pool and a set of scent-marking posts, had begun to behave like a tiger. He patrolled. He scratched at the cedar. The snow leopards, in their reconfigured rocks, climbed for the first time in living memory of the staff. The crowds dwindled briefly during the construction and then, once word spread, returned in numbers that underscored how much the old display had been failing the animals — and, in its way, the visitors who had paid to see them.

questions.q: The director's approach to the renovation is best characterized as
opts: a single dramatic redesign meant to attract media coverage.
a phased, evidence-based sequence in which behind-the-scenes changes precede a public rebuild.
a populist response designed to satisfy the city paper's demands.
a scientific experiment whose outcome was deliberately concealed from the public.
questions.why: The second paragraph describes a measured, multi-phase plan beginning with invisible enrichment changes before the eventual enclosure rebuild — phased and evidence-based.

questions.q: The columnist's argument that the money should be redirected is presented as
opts: morally compelling and unanswered by the director.
rhetorically sharp but legally and practically untenable.
the consensus view of the conservation community.
a private complaint that did not appear in print.
questions.why: The director's response punctures the sharper claims by noting that the restricted bequest could not legally have been redirected — sharp tone, weak substance.

questions.q: The final paragraph's emphasis on the cats' new behavior most directly underscores
opts: the financial efficiency of the renovation project.
the gap between the animals' previous existence and what they were capable of when properly housed.
the popularity of large carnivores relative to other zoo residents.
the columnist's eventual change of heart about the project.
questions.why: The behavioral changes — the tiger patrolling, the leopards climbing — show what the old display had been failing to permit, the gap between subsistence and a fuller life.

5.title: Defending the Translator
5.text:
It has become fashionable, in certain corners of literary criticism, to ridicule the translator. The complaint is that the translator does not, by the nature of her work, produce anything original; that her labor is at best a kind of careful copying. The complaint is not new — Borges, in his measured way, fulminated against it sixty years ago — and yet it returns, in successive generations of critics, with the unwearying confidence of a moth that has not yet learned to avoid a candle.

What such criticism cannot gainsay is the actual prose on the page. To translate Mandelstam, or Bashō, or even a relatively prosaic author like Simenon, is not to copy. It is to hone a sentence in English whose syntax must support the gravity of an original whose grammar bears no resemblance to ours. The translator must delineate, in a tongue Mandelstam never learned, an order of words that exalts the same image he exalted; she must find the rhythms that puncture the reader the way the Russian once did. She does not produce a duplicate. She produces, when she succeeds, a parallel.

The more august practitioners of this art rarely write defenses of it. They are too busy. The defenses, when they come, are written instead by readers — by those of us who have, over decades, watched a single foreign poem migrate through three or four English versions, each with its own panoply of choices, until the poem we now know in our language has been winnowed from the failures and triumphs of a chain of working strangers. To call that chain unoriginal is, on the merits, simply false. To call it preachy or trenchant in the wrong directions is fashionable cultural criticism that has not yet been forced to recant any of its claims.

My quarrel with the dismissive view, then, is not that it is rude to a profession I admire. My quarrel is that it underscores, every time it is repeated, a misunderstanding about how literature reaches readers across languages. Without the translator, the foreign poem stays foreign. With her, it becomes evocative in a way the original could not have been to us. That is not copying. That is, if we are honest, much closer to writing.

questions.q: The author's central claim about translation is that
opts: translators should be paid more than they currently are.
translation produces a parallel work of literature rather than a mere copy.
translators are uniquely qualified to write original poetry.
the best translators always work from languages they have lived in.
questions.why: The author explicitly frames a successful translation as a "parallel" rather than a duplicate — the central claim of the piece.

questions.q: The author's tone toward the dismissive critics is best described as
opts: apologetic, conceding the merit of their position while disagreeing.
patient but firm, treating the dismissal as a recurring misunderstanding rather than a serious thesis.
openly furious at the critics by name.
indifferent, treating the dispute as a minor academic matter.
questions.why: The image of the moth that has not yet learned to avoid the candle, paired with the closing argument, conveys patient firmness rather than fury, apology, or indifference.

questions.q: The third paragraph's image of a poem migrating through several English versions over decades primarily serves to
opts: argue that no translation is ever satisfactory.
show that the poem English readers eventually know is the cumulative product of many translators' labor.
introduce a personal anecdote about a particular poem.
criticize publishers for issuing too many competing editions.
questions.why: The migration of a poem through versions, winnowed from failures and triumphs, is offered as evidence of the cumulative, original labor that critics deny.

5.title: The Jockey
5.text:
From the grandstand, racing looks glamorous. The horses are sleek; the silks are bright; the venues themselves — Saratoga in August, Ascot in June — are the kind of places that television cameras have been carefully positioning since before most of us were born. From the saddle, very little of this is true. By the time a jockey reaches the starting gate, the glamour has already subsided into the small, technical predicament of the next two minutes.

Elena Maro had been a jockey for seventeen years. She was small, even for the trade, and her career had been less phenomenal than reliably astute. She had not won a Triple Crown race; she had also, in seventeen years, never been seriously injured, which in her line of work was the more important number. She had honed her judgment over thousands of starts, and she had become known, among trainers, as the rider who would not waver in the final furlong even when the horse beneath her did.

The race that mattered most to her, in retrospect, was not one of the celebrated afternoons. It was an unimportant claiming race at a regional track, on an October Tuesday, with a horse the trainer had assured her would not win. Elena had not been told the ostensible reason — that the connections had hoped to dwindle the horse's value before selling him — and she would not have ridden the race had she known. She rode, instead, the way she always rode. She did not jockey for position with guile so much as wait for the gap that her experience told her would open. It opened. She wrested the lead at the eighth pole, and the horse, against every prediction, won by half a length.

The ensuing dispute did not linger on Elena. The stewards spearheaded an inquiry; the trainer was suspended; the horse was sold for substantially more than the connections had hoped. Elena herself was courteous to every reporter and admitted nothing she had not been told. She returned, the following Saturday, to a less photographed venue and a less interesting horse. What outsiders never quite understood about her career was that the import of any single race, in her own valuation, was very small. She had reverence only for the work itself — for the steady, unglamorous discipline of staying upright on an animal that weighed twelve hundred pounds and did not always agree with her about where it wanted to go.

questions.q: The passage's portrayal of Elena most directly challenges the assumption that
opts: racing is a sport dominated by male jockeys.
the most successful career in racing is the most spectacular one.
regional tracks produce poorer riders than major venues do.
horses cannot be trained to respond to specific riders.
questions.why: The passage emphasizes that Elena's career was reliable rather than phenomenal, and that her own valuation of any single race was small — challenging the equation of success with spectacle.

questions.q: Elena's behavior in the disputed October race is best understood as
opts: a deliberate effort to embarrass the horse's connections.
the routine application of her usual riding judgment, in the absence of the information that would have made her decline.
an attempt to attract attention from the major tracks.
a calculated gamble made to win a private bet.
questions.why: The passage states she had not been told the ostensible reason for the race and rode "the way she always rode" — routine judgment without the information that would have changed her decision.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the word "import" most nearly means
opts: an article brought from a foreign country.
the act of bringing something into a competition.
significance or weight.
a measure of audience interest.
questions.why: Elena's valuation of any single race "was very small" — "import" is contrasted with the steady discipline she actually values, meaning significance or weight.

5.title: The Minister Toppled
5.text:
The minister of the interior had been toppled, by the time the morning papers reached the capital, in the tidy and entirely lawful way the country's parliament reserved for such matters. He had not been arrested. He had not been ridiculed in the chamber. He had simply, on the previous afternoon, lost a confidence vote by four ballots, after which the prime minister had asked for and received his resignation. The august rituals of parliamentary government had been observed throughout.

What the rituals could not delineate was the trenchant struggle that had ebbed and flowed in the cabinet for the better part of a year. The minister had, in his second term, begun to wrest authority from departments outside his nominal portfolio, and the prime minister — too astute to confront him directly and too cautious to wait — had moved with the kind of quiet guile such situations require. By the time the confidence vote was called, the minister's allies had been, one by one, persuaded to absent themselves from the chamber.

In his resignation statement, the minister was defiant. He did not recant any of the policies for which he had been criticized; he did not concede that the government would be improved by his departure. The strident tone surprised even his own supporters, who had hoped for something more measured. "I will not," he said, in a line that punctured an otherwise careful speech, "convert my disagreement with this prime minister into agreement merely because I have lost a vote." His critics fulminated, predictably, that the line proved exactly the arrogance the vote had been intended to address.

A more honest assessment, written by a senior columnist who had covered both men for two decades, appeared in the weekend edition. The minister, she argued, had been competent at the work the country had bestowed on him and had, in the latter part of his tenure, exalted the office in ways that exceeded its proper function. The prime minister, for his part, had been imperative in protecting the cabinet's collective authority — but had also, in the manner of his maneuvering, stymied the kind of open debate that a healthier system would have welcomed. Both men had served the country. Neither, in the columnist's measured judgment, had served it as well as the country had a right to expect. The piece underscored, in its final paragraph, that the dispute was unlikely to subside before the next election, and might not be settled even then.

questions.q: Which of the following best characterizes the columnist's position in the final paragraph?
opts: She defends the minister and condemns the prime minister.
She defends the prime minister and condemns the minister.
She concludes that both men had merits and failings, and that neither served the country adequately.
She refuses to assign any responsibility for the dispute.
questions.why: The columnist credits each man with genuine service while criticizing each — the minister for exceeding the office, the prime minister for stymying open debate — concluding neither served as well as expected.

questions.q: The minister's line about not converting disagreement into agreement is described as having "punctured" his otherwise careful speech because it
opts: introduced an obvious factual error.
broke through the speech's measured surface to reveal an underlying defiance.
directly attacked the prime minister by name.
contradicted policies the minister had long supported.
questions.why: The line is described as defiant in tone within an otherwise careful speech — it punctures the careful surface by exposing the underlying refusal to concede.

questions.q: The passage's account of the prime minister's strategy emphasizes
opts: his open and combative approach to political disputes.
his use of quiet maneuvering to neutralize an internal rival.
his reluctance to defend the cabinet's collective authority.
his eagerness to expose the minister to public ridicule.
questions.why: The prime minister moves "with the kind of quiet guile such situations require" and persuades the minister's allies to absent themselves — quiet maneuvering rather than open combat.

6.title: The Charlatan in the Town Paper
6.text:
When the new wellness clinic opened on Main Street, the editor of the Larkfield Sentinel, who had run the paper for twenty-three years, recognized a charlatan within five minutes of the founder's first interview. The proprietor was loquacious, evasive, and ostentatiously authoritative on subjects he was clearly sketchy about. He spoke of "vibrational realignment" and "cellular memory" with the casual confidence of someone who had read the same three pages of pop neurology that everyone else in his trade had read. The editor smiled, asked his questions, and went home to think.

What to do about him was less obvious than what he was. The paper's traditional comity with local businesses ran deep; a stern column impugning a new arrival would denigrate, by extension, the chamber of commerce that had welcomed him at a ribbon-cutting the week before. The editor's reporters, when consulted, were divided. The youngest, who had not yet shed her alarmist tendencies, wanted to instigate an investigation immediately. The older reporters preferred neutrality — let the man hang himself, they said, on his own claims.

The editor chose a third path. Over six weeks, the paper ran a careful series on the science of the practices the clinic advertised. The articles were not shrill. They were not obstreperous. They named no names. They cited authoritative sources, included germane quotations from doctors at the regional hospital, and dispelled, point by patient point, the spurious claims that any reader of the clinic's brochure would recognize. The proprietor, predictably, complained. He called the editor patronizing and accused the paper of perpetrating a campaign against him.

The series did not close the clinic. Charlatans, the editor knew, are rarely defeated by evidence; they are defeated, when they are defeated at all, by the slow accumulation of patients who have tried the treatment and felt mediocre at best. What the series did was give those patients a vocabulary. By the end of the year, the clinic's complaints to the chamber had become repetitive enough that even its early defenders fell quiet. The proprietor decamped, eventually, to a larger town that had not yet read the Sentinel. The editor, asked about the episode at his retirement dinner the following spring, gave a measured answer. The job of a small-town paper, he said, was not to expose every conclusive fraud but to make the verities of ordinary judgment a little harder to shout down.

questions.q: The editor's strategy is best described as
opts: an immediate front-page denunciation of the proprietor.
an indirect approach that armed readers with information rather than naming the target.
a refusal to engage with the clinic at all.
a series of editorials demanding the proprietor's prosecution.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies the series named no names but dispelled spurious claims point by point — indirect, information-based rather than denunciatory.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the editor's view of how charlatans are eventually defeated?
opts: By legal action initiated by regulators.
By the accumulation of disappointed patients rather than by direct argument.
By media campaigns that name and shame them publicly.
By the indignation of professional bodies.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph states charlatans are defeated by the slow accumulation of patients who tried the treatment and were left feeling mediocre — not by evidence or denunciation.

questions.q: The closing remark — that the paper's job is to make "the verities of ordinary judgment a little harder to shout down" — most directly conveys
opts: a modest but principled conception of what local journalism can accomplish.
a complaint that the paper's resources are too limited for serious work.
an argument that small-town papers should avoid controversy.
a call for new investigative funding.
questions.why: The remark is offered at the editor's retirement dinner as a measured summary of the job — a modest, principled view of what the paper can do.

6.title: The Leached Field
6.text:
The fields outside Pelham, Vermont, look tranquil from the road. They are fenced in cedar; they are mowed twice a summer; they yield, on average, about half the corn that the same acreage yielded thirty years ago. The decline is not endemic to the region. It is the result, hydrologists now believe, of decades of nitrogen leaching from a fertilizer regime that the smaller farms in the area have only recently begun to ameliorate.

The staggering scale of the problem became clear in the late 2010s, when a state survey of well water turned up nitrate concentrations that, in successive towns along the river valley, exceeded federal advisory limits. The detrimental effect on infants and pregnant women had been documented in the medical literature for half a century. What had not been adequately conveyed to the farms whose runoff exerted the greatest pressure on the watershed was that the harm could be, in some hydrological circumstances, irreparable: nitrogen that has leached into deep groundwater can persist for decades, blighting the wells of farms that had nothing to do with the original application.

The response, when it came, was contingent on cooperation that the demographic shifts of the region had made unusually difficult. The older farmers, who had spent their working lives on the land, were sometimes reluctant to harness new methods that they associated with bureaucratic intrusion. The younger farmers, fewer in number, were also fewer in capital, and could not always afford the cover-cropping schedules that the agronomists urged on them. To overstate the willingness of either group to change quickly would have obstructed the realistic conversation that was, by then, imperative.

What helped, in the end, was a small program at the state university that paired senior farmers with the graduate students whose research most directly served the region. The visits were not lectures. The students brought soil-testing kits and asked, germanely, about specific fields the farmers were already worried about. The farmers, in turn, taught the students what no textbook would: which low spots flooded after which kind of rain, where the bedrock came close enough to the surface to limit any deep amendment, what a setback in a given season meant for next year's planting. The collaboration did not close the gap. It made the gap smaller, by an amount that mattered to the wells, the children, and the long, patient work of getting a watershed back from the consequences of a single generation's choices.

questions.q: The passage's description of nitrogen leaching as potentially "irreparable" most directly emphasizes that
opts: the chemical itself cannot be neutralized in laboratory conditions.
harm done in one place can persist for decades and affect farms that did not cause it.
the agricultural sector lacks the technology to address the problem.
regulators have given up on cleaning the watershed.
questions.why: The passage explains that nitrogen in deep groundwater can persist for decades and blight wells of innocent neighbors — durable harm spreading beyond the original cause.

questions.q: The university program described in the final paragraph is presented as effective primarily because
opts: it imposed strict regulations on the older farmers.
it replaced unproductive farms with research stations.
it built two-way exchange between students and farmers around concrete local conditions.
it offered substantial financial subsidies to participating farms.
questions.why: The final paragraph specifies the visits were not lectures: students brought tools and asked specific questions, and farmers taught practical local knowledge — a two-way, concrete exchange.

questions.q: The author's overall assessment of efforts to repair the watershed is best described as
opts: triumphant about a problem now substantially solved.
fatalistic about a problem too large to address.
modest, framing progress as real but partial within a long horizon.
indifferent to the ecological stakes.
questions.why: The closing line says the collaboration did not close the gap but made it smaller "by an amount that mattered" — explicit framing of partial progress over a long horizon.

6.title: Grandfather, Late
6.text:
My grandfather, in the years I knew him as a child, was reliably irascible. The temper was not directed at me — he had, with his only grandson, the patience that elderly men sometimes reserve for the one role they have not yet failed at — but I saw it directed at almost everyone else. He was churlish with waiters, stern with my mother, and openly cantankerous with his younger brother, whose phone calls he would refuse to take for weeks at a stretch. My memories of him from that period are sketchy in the corners but clear in the center: he is at the head of a table, somewhere, complaining about the soup.

He became, very gradually, someone else. The change was not a single conversion but a long erosion, and I was old enough by the end to see it happen in measured increments. The deaths of his closest contemporaries, one each winter for several years, ameliorated the sharp edges in a way that no amount of family persuasion ever had. His later phone calls to his brother, when they finally resumed, were tranquil and lowly, as though they had agreed without speaking that the disputes whose details neither could now remember were not worth the involved labor of recalling.

The last summer of his life, he asked me to help him sort through a box of letters in the attic. We did this in long, easygoing afternoons that fascinated me more than I let on. He had been, in his thirties, a more demonstrative man than the irascible figure I had grown up with. The letters were melancholy in places — his sister had died young, and he had written to a cousin about it with a tenderness I had not known he possessed — but they were not solitary in tone. They were the letters of someone who had once exerted himself, in writing, to mollify the people he loved.

When he died, in the September after that summer, I gave the eulogy. I did not patronize the relatives who had mostly known the cantankerous version. I described, instead, the man in the attic — neither the early demonstrative one nor the later tranquil one, but the longer person who had contained both. The solace I took from that summer, and have taken from it since, is the simplest kind. I had been allowed, briefly, to know him whole.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the change in the grandfather over time was due primarily to
opts: a deliberate program of self-improvement undertaken late in life.
the cumulative effect of losing his close contemporaries.
professional therapy that the family had insisted on.
the repair of a single major dispute with his brother.
questions.why: The second paragraph attributes the easing of his temper to the deaths of his closest contemporaries, one each winter for several years — cumulative loss rather than therapy or self-improvement.

questions.q: The discovery of the letters in the attic functions in the passage primarily as
opts: evidence that the grandfather had once committed an unforgivable act.
a revelation that the irascible figure had earlier been more tender than the narrator knew.
an explanation of the dispute between the grandfather and his brother.
an introduction to a relative who will appear later in the narrative.
questions.why: The letters reveal a more demonstrative younger man and a tenderness about his sister's death — a revelation about an earlier self the narrator had not known.

questions.q: The narrator's eulogy is best understood as
opts: an attempt to disown the irascible side of the grandfather.
an effort to present the grandfather as the sum of his successive selves rather than only the most recent one.
a public rebuke of relatives who had complained about him.
a private letter that was never actually delivered.
questions.why: The narrator describes neither the early demonstrative man nor the later tranquil one but "the longer person who had contained both" — the sum of successive selves.

6.title: The Blighted Orchard
6.text:
The McIntosh orchard outside the village had been the demographic mainstay of the valley for sixty years. Forty acres comprised the working core; another twelve, gone over to neglect after the founder's death, had been the easygoing project of his daughter Helen for the last decade. The neglected acres were blighted. The trees were leaning. Several rows had not yielded a usable apple in five seasons, and the rust on the lower branches had begun to spread, in successive summers, toward the working core.

Helen was solitary by temperament and not, by any measure, a born orchardist. She was a retired schoolteacher who had inherited a project rather than a passion. What she had, instead, was a stubborn refusal to allow the irreparable. The setback of any single tree did not deter her; the upkeep of the working acres, which she leased to a younger neighbor, generated just enough income to fund the small experiments that ameliorated the blighted ones year by year.

The regional extension agent, who visited every spring, treated her with a respect she found endearing. He had, like all good agents, learned to harness the local knowledge before he offered any imperative of his own. He had pledged, on his first visit, not to recommend any treatment that did not have evidence behind it; he kept that pledge through some years when more aggressive interventions might have been germane. The work that fascinated Helen most was the cover-cropping she did between the rows — a tranquil rotation of clovers and rye that, over five seasons, restored the soil that the original planting had endemically depleted.

The orchard, in any meaningful sense, was not saved. Eight of the twelve neglected acres had to be removed, the trees burned, and the ground rested for three years before any replanting could be attempted. The four remaining acres, however, were yielding usable fruit by the end of the decade — not enough to justify the labor in any commercial sense, but enough to obstruct the simpler narrative of decline. A small share of the harvest was donated, every September, to the food pantry in the next town. Helen herself never spoke of the project as restoration. She spoke, when she spoke of it at all, as upkeep — a word that did not exert any heroic claim, and that suited her.

questions.q: The passage's portrayal of Helen most directly challenges the assumption that
opts: successful land restoration requires a passionate, lifelong commitment to the practice.
older landowners are always more knowledgeable than younger ones.
regional extension services are uniformly unhelpful.
schoolteachers cannot be entrusted with agricultural projects.
questions.why: Helen is described as a retired schoolteacher with neither passion nor expertise, only stubborn refusal to allow the irreparable — challenging the idea that restoration needs lifelong devotion.

questions.q: The extension agent's approach is presented as effective because he
opts: imposed evidence-based protocols regardless of Helen's preferences.
deferred to local knowledge and avoided treatments without evidence behind them.
rotated the orchard's leasing to a more experienced farmer.
secured federal grants that made the restoration financially viable.
questions.why: The third paragraph credits the agent for harnessing local knowledge before offering imperatives and for keeping his pledge to recommend only evidence-based treatments.

questions.q: Helen's preference for the word "upkeep" over "restoration" most directly conveys
opts: her uncertainty about whether the project will succeed.
a modest framing that refuses heroic claims about ordinary, sustained work.
a technical distinction between two horticultural practices.
her resentment of journalists who had visited the orchard.
questions.why: The closing sentence specifies that "upkeep" "did not exert any heroic claim" and suited her — a modest framing of sustained work rather than a triumphant restoration narrative.

6.title: Inside the Memo
6.text:
When the analyst found the memo in a discovery file at three in the morning, she did not feel the rush her colleagues had warned her to expect. She felt only the slow, careful clarity of someone who had been preparing for this moment for nineteen months. The memo, if it was what it appeared to be, would not by itself prove that the company's executives had perpetrated the fraud the regulators were investigating. It would, however, instigate exactly the line of inquiry that the executives had spent the previous two years trying to obstruct.

She took it to her supervisor in the morning. He read it twice, asked two stern questions, and told her to make no copies until he had spoken with counsel. By lunch, she had been moved off the matter. By the next afternoon, she had been told that her concerns, while germane, were not yet conclusive enough to require what counsel called formal escalation. The language was not patronizing in the obvious way. It was patronizing in the more dangerous way that polite institutional language can be when it is trying to mollify someone whose information makes her, for the moment, dangerous.

She did not act shrilly. She did not act alarmingly. She arranged, instead, a meeting with the company's compliance hotline — a covert mechanism the company had ratified in its handbook precisely so that situations like this could be addressed without public reprisal. The hotline staff were professional. They were also, she came to suspect, evasive. The investigator assigned to her case asked careful questions about what she had seen and noticeably fewer about what she had been told to do with it. After three weeks, she received a letter informing her that the matter had been resolved internally and that no further action was required.

It was at that point that she retained outside counsel. The argument she would later make, in the federal complaint that named the executives by title, was simple. The company had not denigrated her concerns to her face; it had, instead, processed them through channels designed to look accountable while ensuring that nothing accountable actually occurred. The spurious neutrality of the compliance machinery had not been an accident; it was, on the evidence, the imperative point of its design. Whether the courts would tear the arrangement asunder — and whether her career would survive the attempt — were questions that, on the morning she filed, she had not yet stopped hoping to answer.

questions.q: The passage's central criticism of the company's compliance system is that it
opts: lacked written procedures for receiving complaints.
was designed to appear accountable while preventing genuine action.
directly threatened employees who raised concerns.
had been recently created and was therefore untested.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph states the spurious neutrality was "the imperative point of its design" — appearing accountable while ensuring nothing accountable occurred.

questions.q: The author's description of the supervisor's language as "patronizing in the more dangerous way" most directly suggests that
opts: the language was openly insulting to the analyst.
polite institutional language can do the work of dismissal more effectively than rudeness.
the supervisor was personally implicated in the fraud.
the analyst had misunderstood her supervisor's intentions.
questions.why: The contrast between obvious patronizing and the more dangerous polite version frames institutional courtesy as a more effective means of dismissal than open rudeness.

questions.q: The analyst's actions throughout the passage are best described as
opts: impulsive responses driven by immediate moral outrage.
deliberate, sequential steps that escalate only after internal channels fail.
covert maneuvers designed to embarrass the company publicly.
the routine handling of an ordinary discovery matter.
questions.why: The analyst takes the memo to her supervisor, then to the hotline, then to outside counsel — a sequential escalation that uses internal channels first.

7.title: The Connoisseur
7.text:
Yves Bonin was the most unassuming culinary connoisseur I have ever met, which was only one of the reasons writers in his field tended to misread him. His dining room in the rue Cler, where he ate four nights a week for thirty years, was nondescript: a table by the window, a single carafe of cold water, an antediluvian copy of Larousse Gastronomique on the side table for settling disputes. From this unpromising perch, he produced, between 1972 and his retirement, the most enduring food writing his country had managed to elicit from any of its supposedly more sumptuous critics.

His fervor for cooking did not present itself as fervor. He was urbane, lighthearted in conversation, inclined to deflect any serious question with a small joke about his own ignorance. The first time I met him, at a cafe in the seventh arrondissement, he asked me three questions about my mother's home cooking before he asked me anything about the restaurant we were ostensibly there to discuss. The questions were not idle. They were, I came to understand later, his way of locating the felicitous detail that would highlight whatever he eventually wrote.

His idiosyncrasies were minor and consistent. He retained, against the advice of every editor he worked with, a fondness for the long compound sentence; he refused to be photographed with the dishes he reviewed; he kept a small notebook in which he recorded only the smells of restaurants, never the tastes, on the theory that smell was the more honest sense and the harder to fake. To call any of this esoteric would have annoyed him. It was, in his view, simply the work — the work that less impassioned writers had stopped doing because the magazines no longer paid for the time it required.

He was sanguine, in his last years, about the state of the profession he was leaving. The pantheon of food writing, he liked to say, would always renew itself, even if it sometimes took a decade for the next exquisite voice to find an editor willing to wait for her. His own legacy, he insisted, was not a list of restaurants saved or destroyed. It was a small set of essays in which a reader could still feel, half a century later, what it was like to sit at a table in Paris in October and to be, for the length of one meal, attentive to nothing else.

questions.q: The passage suggests that writers in Bonin's field misread him primarily because
opts: his published work concealed his real opinions about restaurants.
his unassuming, lighthearted manner did not match the gravity of his actual practice.
he refused to grant interviews to other journalists.
his style of writing had become unfashionable by the time he retired.
questions.why: The opening calls his unassuming manner "only one of the reasons" he was misread; the second paragraph develops the gap between his manner and his serious practice.

questions.q: The narrator's account of Bonin's questions about his mother's cooking is meant to illustrate that Bonin
opts: was uncomfortable discussing professional restaurants.
located the meaningful detail that would later anchor his writing through patient personal questioning.
preferred home cooking to restaurant cooking on principle.
was secretly intending to write about the narrator's family.
questions.why: The questions "were not idle" — the narrator says they were Bonin's way of locating the felicitous detail that would highlight what he eventually wrote.

questions.q: Bonin's claim that his legacy is "not a list of restaurants saved or destroyed" most directly conveys
opts: his frustration at having been ignored by restaurateurs.
a redefinition of his own work as the recovery of attentive experience rather than the issuing of verdicts.
an admission that his reviews had been ineffective.
his hope that the profession would adopt a more aggressive critical stance.
questions.why: Bonin frames the legacy as a small set of essays in which readers can feel what it was like to be attentive at a table — recovery of experience, not verdicts.

7.title: The Slow Disease
7.text:
The disease was degenerative. It had been the central insight of Dr. Martens's predecessor — a woman who had retired from the lab the year before Martens arrived — that the deterioration was not steady but intermittent, with covert phases in which the patient appeared, by every standard test, to have stabilized. Misreading these phases as recoveries had produced, over the previous two decades, a series of spurious clinical reports whose categorical confidence had become, by the time Martens read them, faintly embarrassing to the field.

What Martens had inherited, then, was a research question with a long history of fallacious answers. The patients most susceptible to the misreading were the most highly motivated ones, who reported, sincerely and in good faith, that they felt better. Their intermittent improvements were real. The underlying trajectory of the disease was unaffected. To remedy the misreading would require a more stringent measurement protocol — one that did not rely on subjective self-report and that was not, in any obvious way, esoteric to administer in routine clinical practice.

Martens was conversant with the literature; she was less conversant, when she began, with the institutional politics that any new protocol would necessitate. The senior researchers in the lab were, by temperament, impassioned defenders of the previous decade's methodology. Their objections, when they came, were rarely framed as objections. They were framed as concerns — that the new measurements were too circumstantial, that the proposed sample size was insufficient, that the timing of the proposal was somehow amiss. Martens, who had been warned about this pattern by her predecessor, did not allow the concerns to subdue her. She prepared, instead, the kind of patient documentation that would obviate each of them in turn.

The protocol was approved, eventually, in a form that highlighted the senior researchers' contributions in ways that even Martens found generous. The first results, two years later, were not dramatic. They were, however, viable in a way the previous decade's results had not been. The disease, when measured by the new instruments, behaved exactly as her predecessor had quietly suspected it would. A categorical claim of recovery was no longer possible; a more honest description of the disease, and of the small interventions that might genuinely slow its progress, was now in reach. It was not a remedy. It was the precondition, Martens believed, for any remedy that might one day be found.

questions.q: The central methodological problem the passage describes is that
opts: the disease has no measurable physical markers.
intermittent improvements have been mistaken for genuine recoveries by previous researchers.
patients have refused to participate in long-term studies.
the disease is too rare for statistically meaningful research.
questions.why: The first paragraph identifies the misreading of intermittent improvement as recovery, producing two decades of spurious reports.

questions.q: The senior researchers' resistance to Martens's protocol is best characterized as
opts: open and direct opposition framed in scientific terms.
objections disguised as concerns about details such as timing and sample size.
personal attacks on Martens's qualifications.
silent refusal to engage with the proposal.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies their objections were "rarely framed as objections" but as concerns about circumstantial details, timing, and sample size.

questions.q: The closing distinction between "a remedy" and "the precondition for any remedy" most directly conveys
opts: Martens's pessimism about the disease ever being treatable.
a careful claim that honest measurement is necessary, even if not sufficient, for future treatment.
her intention to leave the field for clinical practice.
a critique of the funding system that pays for research.
questions.why: The final sentences explicitly say the result is not itself a remedy but the precondition for any remedy — necessary but not sufficient, not pessimistic.

7.title: The Neighbor's Garden
7.text:
Mr. Halford had been cantankerous, by my mother's account, since long before the day in 1981 when he had carried his late wife's roses, in a wheelbarrow, across the property line and replanted them in his own back yard. The roses had been thriving in our garden; in his, on a slope where the soil ran shabby and thin, they had not lasted the season. He had never returned what he took. My mother, by the time I was old enough to ask about it, had decided that the equanimity of the next forty years was worth the price of the lost roses.

I inherited the house in my fifties. Mr. Halford was by then in his nineties, alone, and on the verge of giving up the small garden he had retained out of habit. He spoke to me, the first time we met across the fence, in a tone that lurked just on the becoming side of rude — coy, evasive, and unassuming in ways that I came to understand only later were a kind of armor. "Your mother," he said, with the closest thing to a lighthearted gesture I would ever elicit from him, "was kinder than I deserved."

I took to meditating, in the early mornings, on the small bench at the back of my own garden. From there I could see Mr. Halford's roses, which he had eventually replanted on a better-drained corner where they had, against all expectation, made a tranquil comeback. He came out, some mornings, and we would speak for a few minutes about nothing in particular. He was inclined, in those exchanges, to skirt the subject of my mother. I did not press it. The roses had been spoken for.

When he died, in the spring before what would have been his hundredth year, his daughter brought me a small clay pot from his greenhouse. Inside were three rose cuttings. "He wanted you to have these," she said, with an objective composure that did not quite conceal the felicitous tremor in her voice. "He said something amiss had been settled, finally." I planted them on the slope where the originals had once thrived, in soil that was, I suspect, a great deal less shabby than the soil he had once carried them to. They are not yet enduring. But they are growing, and that, for the moment, is enough.

questions.q: The narrator's mother is portrayed as someone who
opts: carefully documented Mr. Halford's misdeeds for legal purposes.
decided that long-term peace with a neighbor outweighed pursuit of a particular wrong.
remained openly hostile to Mr. Halford for the rest of her life.
shared Mr. Halford's interest in gardening as a basis for friendship.
questions.why: The narrator says she decided the equanimity of the next forty years was worth the price of the lost roses — long-term peace over pursuing the wrong.

questions.q: The narrator characterizes Mr. Halford's coyness and evasiveness as
opts: evidence of declining cognitive faculties.
a form of armor whose purpose became clearer to the narrator over time.
a deliberate strategy to avoid returning the roses.
the result of an undisclosed feud with the daughter.
questions.why: The second paragraph names the coy, evasive manner as "a kind of armor that I came to understand only later" — protective, not strategic or pathological.

questions.q: The closing image of the rose cuttings is best understood as
opts: the formal completion of a legal restitution.
a quiet gesture that closes a long-running unspoken matter without announcing it.
an unrelated horticultural anecdote.
a sign that the daughter intends to pursue a further claim.
questions.why: The daughter says he believed something amiss had been settled; the gesture closes the long matter without overt declaration.

7.title: The Treaty
7.text:
By the eighth month of negotiations, the talks in Geneva had settled into the kind of judicious deadlock that diplomatic correspondents enjoy describing and that the diplomats themselves had learned to dread. The two delegations were conversant with each other's positions to the point of weariness. The covert channels that had operated in parallel for the first half of the talks had largely shut down. What remained was the public table, presided over by a Swiss mediator whose pacific temperament had been, by general agreement, the only thing keeping the negotiations alive.

The substantive obstacles were three. The first was the demarcation of the disputed border, which the smaller country regarded as a question of sovereignty and the larger one as a question of administration. The second was the future of the alliance system that had drawn both sides into the original conflict; a univocal commitment from either party to dissolve those alliances was politically impossible at home, and any treaty that failed to circumscribe them would be, in the smaller country's view, antediluvian in the way that recent peace treaties in the region had all proven antediluvian. The third was the question of reparations.

The calumny that flowed through the foreign press during this period was implacable in tone but, on closer reading, surprisingly thin in substance. Neither side, the more careful columnists noted, had accused the other of acts the other had not, in fact, committed. What was being argued about was not the historical record but the categorical narrative each side wanted ratified in the treaty's preamble. The mediator, in a felicitous intervention that even his critics later admired, suggested that the preamble be left to historians and that the treaty itself confine its language to the future.

The treaty, when it was finally signed, was not univocal on any of the three substantive points. It was, instead, judiciously ambiguous on the first two and stringent on the third. Reparations were defined down to the line item; the border question and the alliance question were left in formulations that each side could read, plausibly, as a partial victory. Critics, predictably, called the result shortsighted — a delay rather than a settlement. The mediator, in his closing remarks, did not contest the description. He noted only that delay, in this region's history, had often been the precondition for any settlement at all, and that the talks had at minimum produced a framework no successor would have to dissipate before beginning his own.

questions.q: The treaty's resolution of the three substantive points is best described as
opts: a clear victory for the smaller country on all three.
deliberately ambiguous on the first two points and precise on the third.
a reaffirmation of the prior status quo on every issue.
a temporary ceasefire with no binding commitments.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph explicitly states the treaty was judiciously ambiguous on the first two points and stringent on the third (reparations).

questions.q: The mediator's suggestion to leave the preamble to historians most directly addresses the problem that
opts: the diplomats lacked the historical training to draft accurate language.
each side wanted a categorical narrative of the past ratified in the treaty itself.
the public press had inserted false claims into earlier drafts.
the smaller country had refused to sign any preamble at all.
questions.why: The third paragraph identifies the contested issue as the categorical narrative each side wanted in the preamble; deferring the preamble removes that obstacle.

questions.q: The mediator's response to the charge of shortsightedness is best characterized as
opts: a denial that the treaty has any flaws.
an acceptance of the description coupled with a claim that delay is itself sometimes a precondition for settlement.
a counterattack on the critics' motives.
a refusal to comment on his own work.
questions.why: The mediator does not contest the description but argues delay is often the precondition for settlement — acceptance plus reframing.

7.title: Birds of the Marsh
7.text:
Birding in the salt marsh outside Edisto, in the off-season, is a faintly esoteric pursuit. The serious tourists have gone home; the casual visitors have decided, sensibly, that the gnats are not worth it. Those of us who remain are unassuming about the whole project — eccentric, possibly, in the patient way that requires sitting still for forty minutes in a folding chair to confirm an intermittent flicker that may or may not have been a clapper rail. The agility of the birds we hope to see is exquisite. The agility required to see them is mostly a matter of not moving.

My guide that week was a retired postal carrier named Lonnie, whose sanity, after thirty years of walking the same five rural routes, had been preserved by precisely this hobby. He retained a covert lighthearted streak that the deeper birders in our small circle pretended not to notice. He carried two pairs of binoculars on lanyards around his neck, neither of which was the becoming brand the magazines recommend; both worked perfectly. His scope was older than I was. "You don't pay for glass," he told me on the second morning. "You pay for time. Anyone who tells you different is selling something."

What lurked at the edges of the marsh, in those quiet hours, was more enduring than any single sighting. A great blue heron, tranquil in the shallows, would stand for an entire afternoon as though objective time had circumscribed itself to accommodate his patience. A felicitous gust would, sometimes, elicit a flight of skimmers along the channel — a brief alien moment when the surface of the water seemed not to belong to the ordinary world at all. I tried, on several mornings, to highlight one of these moments in a notebook. The sentences came out shabby. The marsh did not, it turned out, want to be written about.

Lonnie was inclined to agree. "You can keep a list," he said, on the last evening, as we packed up. "That's fine. Lists are honest. Just don't confuse the list with what you saw." I have thought about that distinction often, in the years since. The list is what you can carry home. What you saw is what stays at the edge of the marsh, where you left it, for the next person willing to sit forty minutes in the chair.

questions.q: The passage's central observation about birding is that
opts: it has become inaccessible to amateurs because of expensive equipment.
the rewards depend on patience and presence rather than on equipment or recorded sightings.
it should be reserved for retired professionals with time to spare.
modern birders are losing interest in shorebirds in particular.
questions.why: Lonnie's claim that you pay for time, not glass, and the contrast between the list and what you saw both place the value in patience and presence rather than equipment or records.

questions.q: Lonnie's distinction between "the list" and "what you saw" most directly serves to
opts: criticize amateur birders who keep records.
separate the portable record of a hobby from the experience the record cannot fully contain.
argue that birding journals should be more rigorously scientific.
introduce a new method for organizing field notes.
questions.why: Lonnie says lists are honest but should not be confused with what you saw — the list is what you carry home, the experience is what stays at the marsh.

questions.q: The narrator's admission that her sentences "came out shabby" most directly conveys
opts: that she lacks any literary training.
the limit of language to capture certain kinds of attentive experience.
her embarrassment at being shown up by Lonnie's writing.
the marsh's hostility to all human visitors.
questions.why: The narrator notes the marsh "did not want to be written about" — a recognition that some attentive experience resists capture in language.

8.title: The Anthology
8.text:
Editing a poetry anthology is, on the surface, a meticulous task — a matter of permissions, line breaks, and the consistent application of a chosen orthography. Beneath the surface, the work is intricate in ways that even practiced editors underrate. The editor must decide which voices to include and which to omit; she must decide what range her selections will circumscribe, and what claims her introduction will explicitly avoid. None of these decisions is shallow. All of them, taken together, will determine whether the book becomes an enduring document or merely another seasonal title.

The most common failure of contemporary anthologies is the imposition of a false homogeneity. Editors, indifferent to the actual variety of the period they are surveying, varnish their selections with a single tonal register that makes the poets sound like one another. The trait is easy to ape and difficult to escape; one strong taste, applied across two hundred pages, can flatten a generation. Skeptical readers — and readers should be skeptical of anthologies — learn to recognize the symptom quickly. They look for the friction between consecutive poems, and when they find none, they put the book down.

The better editors do something more difficult. They draw poems whose stability comes from their being unlike each other, and they trust the reader to tolerate the resulting unevenness. The introduction, in such books, is judicious about its claims; it stipulates what the anthology is and is not, and it does not embellish the editor's role with any of the curatorial flourishes that have, in recent decades, become embarrassing. The book that results is more absorbing than the homogenized alternative because the reader, instead of being lulled into a single voice, is asked to encounter fifteen of them.

My own bias, I should confess, is for the genuine over the polished. An anthology that includes a flawed poem because the poem could not have been written by anyone else seems to me more useful than one that excludes the same poem because it does not match the surrounding selections. This is a position I cannot fully defend on theoretical grounds. I can only note that the anthologies I still pull off the shelf, twenty years after I bought them, are uniformly the rougher ones — and that the polished ones, however meticulous, have settled with a kind of indifferent dust into the lower shelves where I rarely look.

questions.q: The author's central criticism of contemporary anthologies is that
opts: they fail to include enough living poets.
they impose a false homogeneity that flattens the variety of the work they survey.
their introductions are too short to explain the editor's choices.
they cost too much for the typical reader to afford.
questions.why: The second paragraph explicitly identifies false homogeneity as the most common failure, with editors varnishing selections in a single tonal register.

questions.q: The author's stated bias for "the genuine over the polished" most directly conveys
opts: a preference for inclusion of distinctive poems even when they are imperfect.
a rejection of all editorial selection.
an objection to anthologies as a form.
a demand that editors include only well-known poets.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph explains the bias: the author prefers a flawed poem that could not have been written by anyone else over one that is excluded for not matching its neighbors.

questions.q: The closing image of dust on the polished anthologies primarily serves to
opts: criticize publishers for poor binding decisions.
support, by personal experience, the claim that rougher anthologies have proven more enduringly useful.
introduce a new genre of literary criticism.
lament the disappearance of physical bookshelves in modern homes.
questions.why: The author offers her shelf as personal evidence that the rougher anthologies remain useful while the polished ones gather dust — the bias supported by lived experience.

8.title: The Cartographer's Apprentice
8.text:
The map shop on Rua das Janelas Verdes, in Lisbon, occupies two rooms behind a butcher and is reached, antiquatedly, by a flight of marble stairs whose handrail has been polished smooth by two centuries of antiquarian visitors. The proprietor, Senhora Estrela, has been the second-generation owner since 1987. Her apprentice, Beatriz, who has been with her for three years, is the absorbing reason I have written this dispatch.

Beatriz studied geography at Coimbra and then, against the trajectory her professors had drawn for her, declined a doctoral fellowship in order to work for Senhora Estrela on a salary that, she will tell you with a small grin, would have founded no fortune. The trade is intricate. A genuine seventeenth-century portolan can be distinguished from a meticulous nineteenth-century forgery only by examining traits the layperson would underrate — the shallow scratching of the rhumb lines, the consistency of the iron-gall ink across the parchment, the explicit traces of a particular cartographer's signature underneath the embellishments that later owners have added.

Senhora Estrela has not delegated much of this work to her apprentice. She has, instead, anchored the apprenticeship in the slowest possible exposure to the material. Beatriz spent her first six months simply cataloguing maps that had already been authenticated, learning the way the genuine examples felt before she was permitted to handle a single questionable item. The judicious progression is more antiquarian, in spirit, than any single map in the shop. "You cannot," the senhora told me, with the air of someone stipulating a house rule that did not require defense, "teach a young person to recognize what is enduring by showing her the recent forgeries first."

The shop is not, in any commercial sense, thriving. The market for antique maps has been in skeptical decline for a decade; the infamy of a few prominent forgery scandals, in London and New York, has made institutional buyers cautious and private buyers timid. But Senhora Estrela is not, in her seventy-second year, attempting to expand. She is attempting only to pass on, intact, an apprenticeship that the trade itself can no longer support without proprietors willing to lose money on the apprentice for three years before she begins to earn her keep. Beatriz, when I asked her whether she would do it again, did not hesitate. "In what other job," she said, "could I learn to read the seventeenth century with my hands?"

questions.q: The passage suggests that Senhora Estrela's training method is distinguished primarily by
opts: the heavy use of digital reference tools.
the deliberate, prolonged exposure to authenticated material before the apprentice handles questionable items.
frequent travel to international map fairs.
the rapid delegation of authentication tasks to the apprentice.
questions.why: The third paragraph describes the slow progression — six months cataloguing authenticated maps before any questionable items — anchored in deliberate exposure.

questions.q: The senhora's remark that one cannot teach a young person to recognize "what is enduring" by showing her "the recent forgeries first" most directly implies that
opts: forgeries are too sophisticated for apprentices to detect.
expert recognition is built from sustained contact with genuine work, against which deviations later become visible.
the apprentice should specialize in forgery detection only.
modern reproductions have no place in any map shop.
questions.why: The remark frames the pedagogical principle: the apprentice must know the genuine deeply before forgeries can be properly understood — recognition built from sustained contact.

questions.q: The author's portrait of the shop is best characterized as
opts: alarmed at the imminent commercial collapse of the antique-map trade.
respectful of a fading mode of training that the trade itself can no longer support.
neutral, simply describing the shop without evaluation.
critical of Beatriz's decision to forgo doctoral study.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph notes the trade can no longer support such apprenticeships and frames the senhora's effort as passing on something intact — respectful of a fading mode.

8.title: Aunt Greta's Last Spring
8.text:
Aunt Greta had been the most sagacious member of our family for as long as I had been old enough to register the distinction. She was amiable without being loquacious, judicious without being callous, and, in the family disputes that periodically festered through the generations, the only voice that could be relied upon to draw a genuine resolution out of a situation everyone else had stopped trying to fix. When she was diagnosed, in her seventy-eighth year, with a slow ailment that the specialists could not cure but could, with discipline, manage, none of us were surprised by the tenacity with which she greeted the news.

She was indifferent to the fuss the family made. She had the wherewithal — money, and what counted as more than money in our family, the moral authority to refuse help she did not want — to organize her own care without delegating it to her grown children. She arranged, with characteristic attention to small things, for an apartment on a single floor; for a friend to drive her to the hospital appointments she would not founder through alone; for a wholesome routine of walks and meals that did not allow her to stagnate, even on the days when stagnation would have been the easier choice.

What I had not expected, in the months I spent visiting her that spring, was how much pleasure she still relished in ordinary days. She had been obstinate, all her life, about not being cosseted; the diagnosis had not changed this trait so much as anchored it. She would sit at the kitchen table with the morning paper, and she would read me the headlines with the same skeptical commentary she had been delivering for decades. She would, on her better afternoons, walk with me to the small park three blocks away and sit on the bench by the fountain. She did not lapse into self-pity. She did not, in my hearing, lament the plight of her own situation.

What she did, in those months, was teach me — not by lecturing, which had never been her way, but by living in front of me a kind of solidarity with her own remaining time. The lesson was enduring without being explicit. I have not been the same since her death, and I do not, when I think of her, feel only loss. I feel, more often, the quiet imperative of her example: that the days one has left are the days one should be most awake to, and that the genuine work of being old is to remain, against every excuse the body offers, a person worth visiting.

questions.q: The passage's portrait of Aunt Greta is best characterized as
opts: an idealized depiction that omits her flaws.
an account of how a long-standing trait of obstinacy was anchored, rather than transformed, by illness.
a critique of family members who failed to support her adequately.
a clinical description of her medical decline.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies the diagnosis did not change her obstinacy about not being cosseted but anchored it — a continuation, not transformation, of long-standing trait.

questions.q: The narrator's observation that Aunt Greta did not "lapse into self-pity" or lament her own plight is intended to
opts: criticize relatives who had been more openly emotional.
characterize the equanimity through which Greta inhabited her remaining time.
suggest that Greta was suppressing genuine feelings to protect others.
introduce a discussion of antidepressant medication.
questions.why: The detail is offered alongside her continued reading of the paper and walks to the park — a portrait of equanimous inhabitation of her remaining time.

questions.q: The closing description of "the genuine work of being old" most directly conveys
opts: a complaint that elderly people are abandoned by their families.
a quiet ethical imperative the narrator has drawn from Greta's example.
a medical recommendation about exercise and diet.
a contrast between Greta and her contemporaries.
questions.why: The narrator describes the lesson as enduring without being explicit and frames it as an imperative drawn from Greta's example — a quiet ethical lesson.

8.title: The Diplomat's Hand
8.text:
Among the diplomats of her generation, Ambassador Reyes was widely held to wield the most judicious hand at a deadlocked negotiating table. Her colleagues — even those who had failed to anchor agreements that she had later salvaged — were not skeptical about this. They were merely curious about the mechanism. She did not, by any explicit account, do anything that her predecessors had not also done. She listened. She circumscribed her own speech to the minimum necessary. She did not, when others had foundered into long, recriminating speeches, allow the discussion to stagnate.

Her asset, on the rare occasions when she chose to describe her own method, was a sagacious refusal to treat any particular formulation as univocal. "Every sentence in a treaty," she once told a class of younger diplomats, "can be read three ways. Two of them are tantamount to what we want, and one of them is tantamount to what they want. The trick is not to draft a sentence that admits only the first two; the trick is to draft a sentence that does not ratify the third." The remark was quoted often, and often misunderstood. What she meant was not that ambiguity is itself a virtue. What she meant was that intricate negotiations require a kind of judicious tolerance for readings that one has not personally chosen.

The negotiation that established her reputation was a trade dispute that had hampered her country's relationship with a major partner for three years. Her predecessor had attempted to ordain a single, comprehensive framework; the framework had stipulated more than the partner could accept, and the talks had foundered. Reyes inherited the file, decoupled the trade question from a security question that had been entangled with it, and proposed a more modest text. The text did not solve the underlying disagreement. It produced, instead, a stability that allowed both governments to claim a partial result and to pursue the larger question on a longer trajectory.

Critics, of whom she had a reasonable share, called the agreement obstinate in its modesty — a refusal to attempt the comprehensive settlement that the moment had, they argued, made possible. Reyes did not respond to such criticisms publicly. To her younger colleagues, in private, she sometimes underrated her own role. "The settlement that lasts," she liked to say, "is the settlement that the next ambassador does not have to undo. Anything more comprehensive than that is, on average, a settlement someone will eventually undo." Whether the assessment was modest or hard-headed depended, as so much in her profession depended, on which sentence one chose to read it through.

questions.q: Ambassador Reyes's negotiating principle, as described in the second paragraph, is best summarized as
opts: the deliberate creation of unambiguous treaty language.
a tolerance for treaty language that admits readings she has not personally chosen, provided it does not ratify the opposing reading.
an insistence that ambiguity is always preferable to clarity.
a refusal to engage with treaty drafting at all.
questions.why: The second paragraph explains that the trick is not to admit only one's own reading but to avoid ratifying the opposing one — tolerance for unselected readings paired with a single firm exclusion.

questions.q: The trade dispute negotiation is presented as successful primarily because Reyes
opts: imposed a comprehensive framework on the trading partner.
decoupled an entangled question and accepted a partial settlement that allowed both sides to continue.
allowed the dispute to remain unresolved indefinitely.
secured an explicit admission of fault from the other government.
questions.why: The third paragraph credits her with decoupling the security question from the trade question and producing a partial, sustainable text — not comprehensive resolution.

questions.q: Reyes's remark that the lasting settlement is the one "the next ambassador does not have to undo" is best understood as
opts: a defense of inaction in the face of opportunity.
an argument that durability, not comprehensiveness, is the proper standard for diplomatic success.
a personal slight directed at her predecessor.
an admission that her own settlement is unlikely to last.
questions.why: The remark privileges the durability of a settlement as the relevant test, in contrast to the comprehensiveness her critics demanded — a methodological standard, not inaction or insult.

8.title: The Edge of the Reef
8.text:
From the dive boat, the reef looks shallow and unremarkable — a darker patch in otherwise pale water, the kind of feature any layperson would underrate. From the surface, with a mask, the reef begins to gleam in the slanting morning light. From ten meters down, it is the most absorbing biological structure most divers will ever see in their lives.

My guide on the trip was a marine biologist named Lucinda who had spent eight seasons mapping a single quarter-kilometer of reef off the southern Belizean coast. Her method was meticulous. She did not embellish what she saw; she stipulated, before each dive, exactly which species she would be tracking, and she kept her observations consistent across the year so that her records of any single colony's trajectory would be comparable from season to season. The intricate work of distinguishing one staghorn fragment from its neighbors had become, for her, a kind of meditative judicious labor. "You cannot help a reef," she said on our first evening, "if you cannot tell which corals were here last year."

What mesmerized me, on my first dive with her, was not the famous fish. It was a single yellow gorgonian — a sea fan as wide across as my arms — anchored to a knob of older coral, swaying in the surge in a way that I would have called wholesome had I not been afraid the word would sound shallow. Lucinda watched it with me for a long minute. "That one is doing fine this year," she said when we surfaced. "Last year it was indifferent. The year before it had nearly vanished. We do not yet know why."

The reef, I came to understand over the week, had a stability that the popular literature on reef collapse had taught me not to expect. Reefs do collapse. They are also, in some places, drawing themselves back from collapses they appeared to have foundered in. Lucinda was skeptical of any single explanation. She did not decouple her hopes from her data, but she did not allow her hopes to write the conclusions either. "My job," she said, on the last morning, "is to make explicit what the reef is actually doing. The trait it has, most years, is a kind of patience. It is more patient with me than I deserve. The least I can do is be patient back."

questions.q: The passage's portrayal of Lucinda's method most directly emphasizes
opts: the importance of dramatic narrative in scientific outreach.
the patient, comparative observation of specific organisms across seasons.
the use of advanced underwater equipment to expand survey range.
the prioritization of charismatic species over less visible ones.
questions.why: The second paragraph describes consistent stipulated observations of specific species so that any colony's trajectory can be compared across seasons — patient, comparative observation.

questions.q: Lucinda's account of the gorgonian's three-year history primarily serves to
opts: illustrate that reef organisms cannot be reliably tracked.
complicate any simple narrative of either reef collapse or reef recovery.
demonstrate the limitations of underwater photography.
introduce a critique of marine tourism.
questions.why: The gorgonian's near-vanishing, indifference, and recovery across three years complicates a single trajectory and supports the claim that some reefs draw themselves back from apparent collapse.

questions.q: Lucinda's closing remark — that her job is to be patient with the reef as it is patient with her — is best understood as
opts: a romantic flourish disconnected from her actual practice.
a methodological commitment that disciplines her hopes by her data.
an expression of frustration with the slow pace of research.
a complaint about the lack of public funding for reef science.
questions.why: The closing paragraph specifies she does not decouple hope from data but does not allow hope to write conclusions — patience as a methodological discipline.

9.title: The Acolyte
9.text:
When I was nineteen I became, for two years, an acolyte of a man who called himself a teacher. He was not, in retrospect, a sublime mind. He was a patent fraud who had learned to dissemble well enough that the credulous among us, of whom I was one, mistook a polished aphorism for a deep thought. He spoke in bromides about presence and salvation, repeating the same dozen lines in different rooms, and I copied them down as if I were transcribing scripture.

The enticement, looking back, was not what he said. It was the room he had built. There were forty of us in any given month, mostly novices to spiritual practice, and the perennial warmth of belonging was a thing I had never had at college. He was clever about this. He cajoled the doubters with private attention, and he encouraged the rest of us to discard the friendships we had brought with us, on the grounds that those friendships were vestiges of a self we were trying to leave behind.

What finally perplexed me, in the second year, was a small thing. A woman in our circle had given him a substantial sum of money for what she believed was an upcoming retreat. The retreat was canceled. The money was not returned. He explained the discrepancy with a story so blatantly improvised that even I, in my enthusiasm, could feel the gap between the words and the facts. I asked, mildly, about the veracity of his account. He looked at me for a long moment, and then exaggerated a smile. The room went quiet. I understood, with the kind of clarity that arrives once and does not leave, that I had been gullible in the most ordinary way.

I went home a week later, aghast not at him but at myself. He is still teaching, I gather, in another city. The friends I had discarded took me back without comment. I do not, even now, judge the others harshly. The room had been warm, and the bromides had been comforting, and the longing for salvation had been honest, even when its object was not.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the narrator's final attitude toward the experience?
opts: Bitter denunciation of everyone involved.
Self-criticism balanced by sympathy for fellow followers.
Indifference, having moved on without reflection.
Renewed admiration for the teacher despite his flaws.
questions.why: The closing paragraph names the narrator as "aghast not at him but at myself" yet refuses to judge the other followers harshly — a self-critical stance paired with sympathy.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the teacher's effectiveness rested primarily on
opts: the originality and depth of his ideas.
the social environment of belonging he constructed for newcomers.
his ability to predict the future for individual followers.
the financial resources he distributed to his circle.
questions.why: The second paragraph explicitly names "the room he had built" — the warmth of belonging — rather than the content of his sayings, as the source of his pull.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "vestiges of a self we were trying to leave behind" is most directly used to describe
opts: old religious texts the group rejected.
the friendships followers were urged to abandon.
remnants of clothing and possessions discarded on entry.
memories of childhood the teacher discouraged.
questions.why: The phrase appears in the discussion of friendships followers were told to discard; the friendships were the vestiges he reframed as obstacles.

9.title: Restoring the Imperial Hall
9.text:
When the conservation team began work on the old imperial hall in 2018, they found the building in a state of decrepitude that even the most pessimistic of the extant surveys had failed to capture. The roof had partially collapsed. The hall's once-staple lacquer columns were eaten through at the base. The upper galleries had become, over a century of neglect, scant more than a vestige of the original carpentry — a few crossbeams, two doorframes, and a single balustrade still bearing the lattice of the imperial mason's hand.

The team's lead conservator, Dr. Han, was conscientious in a way the project's funders sometimes found exasperating. She refused to discard salvageable timber, even when wholesale replacement would have been faster and cheaper.
