"The forebears who cut these beams," she liked to say, "husbanded the trees for forty years before the felling. We will not exaggerate our own urgency above their patience." The ministry, which subsidized the project, was compliant with this principle on most days, although the budget meetings became, by the third winter, perennial battles over how many ancillary repairs would be permitted in any given quarter.

The distinctive challenge, Dr. Han would later write, was distilling from the surviving fragments a model accurate enough to guide the new construction. There was no embryonic plan in the archives — no original blueprint, no contemporary drawing — and the conservators were forced to read the building itself: the angle of a chisel mark, the curve of a tile, the residue of pigment on a beam. From these, in a process that occupied two full years before any new wood was cut, they distilled a working reconstruction.

The hall reopened last spring. It is not a perfect copy of the eighteenth-century original; no honest conservator would claim such a thing is possible. But the visitors who walked through it on the first weekend reported a quality the project's critics had not anticipated. The hall felt, in a way that surprised even Dr. Han, like a resurgent room — not a reconstruction, exactly, but a continuation, by hands that had taken the forebears' instructions seriously.

questions.q: The passage suggests that Dr. Han's central methodological commitment was to
opts: accelerate restoration by replacing damaged materials wholesale.
preserve continuity with the original builders' practice even at the cost of speed.
produce an exact replica indistinguishable from the eighteenth-century original.
document the project for academic publication above all else.
questions.why: The second paragraph's quoted principle — refusing to discard salvageable timber, citing the forebears' patience — defines her commitment as continuity with original practice, not speed.

questions.q: The absence of an "embryonic plan in the archives" is significant in the passage because it
opts: demonstrates that the original builders were illiterate.
forced the team to derive their reconstruction from the surviving fabric itself.
led the team to abandon the project temporarily.
explains why the ministry refused to subsidize the work.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies that without a blueprint the conservators "were forced to read the building itself" — making the absence of plans the reason for the fabric-based method.

questions.q: In context, the closing description of the hall as "resurgent" most nearly conveys
opts: that the hall has surpassed its original architectural significance.
that visitors experienced it as a living continuation rather than a sterile copy.
that the building has been repurposed for modern political use.
that the original builders had foreseen its eventual restoration.
questions.why: The final sentence glosses "resurgent" with "a continuation, by hands that had taken the forebears' instructions seriously" — a living continuation rather than a copy.

9.title: The Manuscript
9.text:
The manuscript that arrived at the rare-books library that autumn had baffled three previous scholars and was, when it reached me, on the verge of being shelved as uninformative. It was a thin codex of imperial-era origin, its cover stamped with a seal that did not square with any extant catalogue, and its text was a kind of equivocal prose: at first glance an aphorism collection, at second glance a private diary, at third glance neither.

My first month with it was unproductive. I tried to parse the syntax against the standard grammars and found that the author had used several patently irregular constructions; the lexicon, when I checked it, was conscientious enough to be the work of an educated hand but contained outlandish coinages I could find nowhere else. A novice in the field would have been forgiven for concluding that the manuscript was a fake. I am not a novice, and I had reasons — the paper, the binding, the stitching — to believe its veracity. But I could not yet distill from the text any account of what its author had been trying to say.

The breakthrough, when it came, was a small one. I had been reading the manuscript as continuous prose. One afternoon I noticed that the irregular constructions clustered, and that they marked, at intervals, what might be the boundaries of separate entries. The text was not a treatise. It was a sequence of short, dated reflections — a notebook, essentially — in which the author, who had clearly understated her own learning, addressed an absent correspondent in language that had been deliberately disguised. The far-fetched coinages were not coinages at all. They were a code, and the code, once I had identified one term, unlocked the rest within a week.

I have not yet published. The temptation to exaggerate the discovery is real, and I will not give in to it; one cannot discard the dignity of the original by overselling its rediscovery. But the manuscript, which had been on the verge of being shelved, will instead be the subject of a long and patient edition. The author, whoever she was, has waited four hundred years. She can wait a little longer for the right book.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the scholar's eventual breakthrough?
opts: Discovering that the manuscript was a modern forgery.
Recognizing that the irregularities marked entry boundaries and concealed a code.
Locating an external dictionary that defined every coinage.
Determining that the author was a member of the imperial court.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies that the irregular constructions marked entry boundaries and that the coinages were a code, identifiable once the structure was seen — that is the breakthrough.

questions.q: The scholar's decision not to publish immediately is best understood as
opts: evidence that he doubts the manuscript's authenticity.
a refusal to oversell the discovery at the cost of the original.
a tactical delay to secure better academic credit.
a concession to the previous scholars who failed to read it.
questions.why: The closing paragraph names the scholar's worry directly: "one cannot discard the dignity of the original by overselling its rediscovery" — refusal to exaggerate.

questions.q: In context, the description of the scholar as "not a novice" functions primarily to
opts: establish his authority for ruling the manuscript authentic despite irregularities.
introduce a contrast with younger scholars he plans to mentor.
explain why he was assigned this particular project.
criticize the three earlier scholars for incompetence.
questions.why: The phrase appears precisely where the text might otherwise be dismissed as fake; his expertise is what justifies trusting the physical evidence over the textual irregularities.

9.title: The Dog at the Gate
9.text:
The dog at the back gate had been, by any reasonable description, ferocious. The neighbors said so. The mailman said so. My mother, who had a predilection for stray animals and a tender record of taking them in, was the first person on our block who would not approach it. "That one," she said, after a single visit, "will bite the hand that feeds it." I was twelve, credulous in the way twelve-year-olds are about animals, and I disagreed.

The dog had been chained to a post by a previous owner who had moved away in haste. Whatever benevolent impulse had led the new tenants to leave food in a bowl had been undercut by their tepid willingness to engage further. The animal cowered when approached, and then, when the approach continued, lunged with a violence that left the few visitors who had attempted any reconciliation aghast. The stigma of being known as a biter had attached to the dog within a week.

My method was patient. I did not approach. I sat, conscientious to the point that my mother found it irritating, on a stump fifteen feet away, with a book and an apple, every afternoon for two months. The dog watched me, impassive at first, then perplexed, then — by the sixth week — with an interest I could not have cajoled into existence by any other means. I did not feed her. I did not speak to her. I only failed, day after day, to be the threat she had learned to expect.

What finally happened was undramatic. One evening she walked the length of her chain, sat down at its limit, and looked at me with what I can only call an irenic patience. I went home that night and told my mother that I thought the dog was ready. She came with me the next morning, and within a week we had, between us, untied the chain and walked the dog into our kitchen. She lived with us for nine years. She never bit anyone. The knotty problem of her past did not, in the end, incur a future; she had only needed someone willing to be unhurried, and we had only needed the scant patience of two months to give it.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the central insight of the passage?
opts: Aggressive animals can never be safely brought into a family home.
An animal's reputation can persist long after the conditions that created it have changed.
Children are better than adults at training neglected dogs.
Patience can sometimes accomplish what attempts at active reconciliation cannot.
questions.why: The narrator emphasizes that he did not feed or speak to the dog — only "failed... to be the threat she had learned to expect" — and the conclusion frames patience itself as the working agent.

questions.q: The narrator's mother is portrayed in the passage as
opts: indifferent to stray animals in general.
experienced enough with strays to recognize a danger she would not engage.
hostile to the narrator's interest in the dog.
willing to confront the dog despite her own fears.
questions.why: The first paragraph notes her tender record of taking in strays, then says she would not approach this one — establishing her as experienced enough to know which strays to leave alone.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "failed, day after day, to be the threat she had learned to expect" most directly conveys that the narrator's effectiveness lay in
opts: his physical inability to harm the dog.
his deliberate refusal to confirm the dog's expectations of danger.
his ignorance of how dangerous the dog actually was.
his strict adherence to the mother's training instructions.
questions.why: The phrasing makes the failure deliberate — sustained over two months — and frames it as a refusal to confirm the dog's prior expectation of threat.

9.title: The Mayor's Office
9.text:
By the time the city paper finally published its investigation into the mayor's office, the malfeasance had been simmering, in plain sight, for the better part of a year. There had been a row at the council in November. There had been a shoddy procurement decision in February that even the mayor's own staff had been unable to defend. There had been the patent appropriation of a redevelopment fund for purposes that bore no resemblance to its authorized use. The blatant nature of the misconduct was, in fact, what had so long discouraged the press: the conduct seemed too obvious to be true, and the editors had been wary of incurring a libel suit by parsing what they could not yet fully document.

The reporter who finally broke the story, Naomi Kessler, had been adamant, for months, that the veracity of the rumors could be established by ordinary records work. She did not exaggerate her sources; she did not lionize her own work in the newsroom. She simply requested, week after week, the kind of contracts and emails that municipal law required to be public, and she filed quiet appeals when those requests were declined. The mayor's office tried, at various points, to cajole her into dropping the line of inquiry — first with offers of background interviews, then with reminders of the impending election cycle.

When the story ran, it accentuated rather than overstated the evidence. The headline was modest. The opening paragraph named no crimes. What the piece did, in its slow accumulation of dates and signatures, was make it impossible to discard the documents as ambiguous. The mayor resigned within two weeks. The state attorney general's office opened an investigation that would, eighteen months later, end in two convictions and a third plea agreement.

The debacle is now, predictably, treated as a triumph of investigative reporting. Kessler is uncomfortable with the description. She advocates, in the few public talks she has given since, for a less heroic reading. The story was not, she insists, a feat of journalistic genius; it was the result of being aghast enough at routine corruption to keep filing the routine paperwork that exposes it. The city's other reporters, she points out, could have done the same. Most of them, for one reason or another, did not.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the press was slow to investigate primarily because
opts: the mayor had personally threatened individual reporters.
the misconduct seemed so obvious that editors feared exposure to libel without full documentation.
the city paper had financial ties to the mayor's office.
no records of the misconduct existed in public form.
questions.why: The first paragraph explains the delay: "the conduct seemed too obvious to be true, and the editors had been wary of incurring a libel suit by parsing what they could not yet fully document."

questions.q: Kessler's preferred account of how the story was obtained emphasizes
opts: the bravery of confidential sources within the mayor's office.
the patient and unglamorous use of routine public-records requests.
her access to documents leaked by federal investigators.
the pressure exerted by other newspapers on the mayor.
questions.why: The second and final paragraphs specify that she requested public records week after week and frames the work as routine paperwork rather than journalistic genius.

questions.q: The author's tone toward Kessler in the final paragraph is best characterized as
opts: skeptical of her self-effacement.
respectful of her insistence on a non-heroic interpretation.
openly dismissive of investigative journalism generally.
indifferent to the broader civic implications.
questions.why: The author reports Kessler's view at length and gives her the closing observation about other reporters, treating her self-effacing account with respect rather than skepticism.

10.title: The Beekeeper
10.text:
Vera kept eleven hives at the edge of a bucolic field that her grandfather had cleared in 1949. The work was laborious and, by any modest reckoning, not economic; she sold the honey at a market where the customers were fervent but few. What kept her at it, year after year, was something less perceptible than profit. The hives were the only acoustic instrument she had ever needed. In April she could tell, by the synchronous hum that rose from the boxes when she lifted a lid, whether a colony had survived the long months in which the bees had hibernated.

A perfect spring afternoon at the apiary was a serene thing. The bees congregated in shallow dishes of water she had set out for them. The brood comb, when she eased it into the light, was a spongy lattice of dainty white cells. The denizens of the hive moved over its surface in a moderate, unhurried rhythm that had, over the seasons, etched itself into the rhythm of her own attention. She did not yearn for any other landscape. She had wanted, as a young woman, to live in cities; the city had been, to her surprise, a tender disappointment.

Honey is perishable in the long sense — sealed properly, it lasts decades — but the bees themselves are not. A queen, if she is a good one, will lay for three years and then begin to fail; a worker may live six weeks in summer. The renewal of the colony is constant, and the beekeeper's work is to support that renewal without imposing on it. Vera disliked the panache of beekeepers who treated the hive as a managed enterprise. The hive, she liked to say, manages itself; the human role is to leave room for what is already happening.

In October, when the field had begun to brown and the days had shortened past the point where the bees would forage, Vera would close each hive with a thin board of cedar. The boxes were quiet then, but not empty. Inside, the colony was clustering — synchronous, warm, alive. The hum was no longer audible at the lid. It had moved, in a way she had stopped trying to explain to visitors, into the wood itself.

questions.q: The passage's central claim about beekeeping, in Vera's view, is that
opts: modern hive technology has made the work obsolete.
the beekeeper's role is to support a colony that fundamentally manages itself.
honey production is the most economically reliable form of farming.
successful beekeeping requires constant intervention in the colony's affairs.
questions.why: The third paragraph states Vera's view directly: the hive "manages itself; the human role is to leave room for what is already happening."

questions.q: Which of the following best characterizes Vera's earlier life as described in the second paragraph?
opts: She had tried urban life and found it quietly disappointing.
She had inherited the apiary as a young woman against her wishes.
She had failed at city work and retreated to the country in shame.
She had always intended to become a beekeeper from childhood.
questions.why: The second paragraph notes she had wanted to live in cities and that the city had been "a tender disappointment" — tried and quietly found wanting.

questions.q: In context, the closing image of the hum having "moved... into the wood itself" most directly conveys
opts: that the colony has moved to a different physical location.
that winter activity is real but no longer audible from outside the hive.
that Vera has begun to imagine sounds that are not actually there.
that the hive has been damaged and is no longer functional.
questions.why: The paragraph specifies that the colony is clustering "synchronous, warm, alive" — real activity, just no longer audible at the lid.

10.title: The Hoax
10.text:
The hoax that ran in the town's weekly paper in 2003 was, in the cold light of subsequent investigation, a moderate piece of work. The trickster — a recently fired editorial assistant — had filed a false obituary for a local man who was very much alive, attaching to it a long and patently fabricated account of an act of wartime heroism the man had never performed. The piece ran on a Wednesday. By Friday, the canard had been picked up by two regional papers, and a small but fervent online community had begun to circulate the story as evidence of forgotten valor.

The local man, when reporters reached him at home, recoiled visibly from the attention. He had not, he said, done any of the things attributed to him; he had been a clerk in the supply corps, and he had spent the war filing requisition forms in a town that the canard's author had located, blatantly, on the wrong continent. The reproach he directed at the paper was articulate but moderate. He was not, he said, hoodwinked or harmed; he was simply embarrassed for everyone involved, including the man who had written the piece.

The paper's editor, fraught with the kind of regret that comes too late to undo anything, attempted at first to stonewall the regional press. He refused to divulge the assistant's name; he declined to characterize the piece as fabricated. This phase lasted three days, until a senior reporter at one of the regional papers obtained the original submission email and the gullibility of the paper's verification process became, itself, the story. The watershed moment, by everyone's account, was the editor's eventual admission, in a perceptible and unguarded interview, that he had not asked any of the questions a competent editor was supposed to ask.

The trickster's reprehensible career as a journalist was over within a week. The paper's reputation, more durably tarnished, did not diminish to nothing — small papers are forgiven much, in towns where they are still read — but it never fully recovered the standing it had held before. The local man, when asked about the affair years later, declined to dissemble: the piece, he said, had been a stupid one, and the paper had been stupid to run it, and that was the most he had to say about it.

questions.q: The passage indicates that the deepest damage to the paper's reputation came from
opts: the original false obituary itself, written by the trickster.
the editor's three-day attempt to stonewall press inquiries.
the senior reporter's investigation at a regional paper.
the local man's complaints about being misrepresented.
questions.why: The third paragraph identifies the editor's stonewalling and the gullibility of the verification process as the watershed — the point at which the paper's failure, not the trickster's lie, became the story.

questions.q: The local man's response to the false obituary, as described in the passage, is best characterized as
opts: indignant and litigious.
amused and gracious.
embarrassed but measured rather than retributive.
uncertain about whether the events described had really occurred.
questions.why: The second paragraph specifies that he recoiled but was "articulate but moderate," embarrassed for everyone, not personally vengeful — measured rather than retributive.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "perceptible and unguarded interview" most nearly describes an interview that was
opts: conducted secretly without the editor's full awareness.
noticeably candid in a way that broke from the editor's earlier evasions.
limited to a small group of subscribers.
transcribed inaccurately by the regional press.
questions.why: The interview is contrasted with the prior three days of stonewalling and is the moment at which the editor admits he failed — a candor noticeably different from before.

10.title: Recording the Last Speakers
10.text:
Linguistic anthropology has, in the last two decades, recast its account of language demise. The older models, which treated the loss of a language as a roughly synchronous process — speakers diminishing in count until none remain — have been replaced by something more fraught and less tidy. A language can be alive in the modest sense for years after its last fluent speaker has died, persisting in the songs of grandchildren who know the melodies but cannot articulate the lyrics, or in the names that still etch the hills of a place no longer inhabited by its original denizens.

My own fieldwork, which has been laborious in the most ordinary sense, has been an effort to record the last fluent speakers of a coastal language whose community had been forcibly relocated three generations ago. The recordings are long; the speakers are tender; the work, on most days, is moderate listening punctuated by the perceptible sadness of someone who has no one left to converse with in their own first tongue. I do not pretend to be evenhanded about the colonial history that produced the situation. But the recordings are, I have learned, more useful when they are made without recasting them as evidence in any one argument.

What the recordings safeguard is something narrower than language and something broader than vocabulary. A grammar can be reconstructed from a few hundred hours of careful interviews; a dictionary can be assembled in a year. What cannot be reconstructed, once it is gone, is the synthesis of habit and idiom that allows a fluent speaker to make a joke. The jokes, in my project, have been the hardest material to capture. The speakers yearn to be funny in a register that no living audience can fully receive, and the laughter, when it comes, is bolstered mostly by my own goodwill rather than by genuine comprehension.

The primacy of revival programs in the public conversation has, on the whole, been a renewal worth supporting. Children in the community are now learning the language in modest numbers, and a few of them will become, in time, real speakers. But the recordings are not for them. The recordings are for the people who already lived this language and who have a right, while they are still living, to be heard speaking it as fluently as they once did. Whether anyone, eventually, can hear them as they meant to be heard is a question I have learned not to ask.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the central methodological claim of the passage?
opts: Language loss is best modeled as a single synchronous event.
The recordings are most useful when not recast as evidence for any single argument.
Grammar reconstruction has been the primary aim of the fieldwork.
Revival programs in schools should be the focus of all linguistic work.
questions.why: The second paragraph states this directly: the recordings are "more useful when they are made without recasting them as evidence in any one argument."

questions.q: The author identifies which of the following as the hardest material to record?
opts: Place names and geographical vocabulary.
Songs whose melodies have outlived their lyrics.
The synthesis of habit and idiom that produces jokes.
Long historical narratives told from memory.
questions.why: The third paragraph names jokes — "the synthesis of habit and idiom" — as the hardest material to capture.

questions.q: The closing paragraph distinguishes the purpose of the recordings from
opts: the eventual benefit they may provide to children in revival programs.
the colonial history the author refuses to address.
the goals of competing anthropological projects.
the personal interests of the author as a researcher.
questions.why: The closing paragraph explicitly states the recordings are "not for them" — the children in revival programs — but for the existing speakers, distinguishing the two purposes.

10.title: The Quiet Surgeon
10.text:
Dr. Imran Sayid had been, throughout his thirty years at the teaching hospital, conspicuously laconic. He did not lecture his residents in the long form; he abbreviated his case discussions to the smallest set of facts that the situation required. His evenhanded reviews of trainee performance were, by the standards of the surgical service, modest in word count and exemplary in usefulness. "He says less," one resident wrote in an evaluation, "than any attending I have worked with, and I have learned more."

The profession, predictably, had not always known what to do with him. Surgeons of his generation had been encouraged to articulate their reasoning in the operating theater, partly to teach and partly to bolster the confidence of the team. Imran's silences during difficult procedures had, in his early years, been read as a sign of arrogance or even of acute uncertainty. Neither was true. He had simply concluded, as a young attending, that the daunting task of operating safely on a fraught field was diminished, not aided, by the panache of running commentary.

What distinguished him, beyond the silences, was an unusual tenderness toward his patients in the moments before anesthesia. He yearned, his nurses said, to safeguard for each patient the small dignity of being addressed by name, in full sentences, on what might be the last morning of their conscious life. He never abbreviated those exchanges. Whatever moderate efficiency he imposed on his teaching, he refused to impose on the patient's first ten minutes in his care.

When the residents began, in his last years, to compile a small handbook of his practice, they were perplexed by how little they could write down. Imran's surgical method was a synthesis of judgments he had not bothered to make explicit even to himself. The handbook, when it appeared after his retirement, was modest, blunt, and only forty pages long. The opening sentence — which the residents had voted unanimously to put in his own words, as he had once said it on a fervent night during a difficult case — read: "The patient is the operation. Everything else is preparation." It is, by all accounts, the most quoted line in the surgical service to this day.

questions.q: The passage suggests that Dr. Sayid's silence during procedures was misinterpreted by his early colleagues as
opts: a humble acknowledgment of his limits.
either arrogance or acute uncertainty about the case at hand.
evidence of a hearing impairment.
deliberate cruelty toward the surgical team.
questions.why: The second paragraph names the misreading directly: his silences "had been read as a sign of arrogance or even of acute uncertainty."

questions.q: The contrast between Sayid's general efficiency and his behavior with patients before anesthesia is best understood as
opts: an inconsistency he was unaware of.
a deliberate exception that protected the patient's dignity.
an attempt to compensate for his rudeness elsewhere.
a requirement imposed on him by hospital policy.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies he refused to abbreviate the patient's first ten minutes, framing it as a deliberate principle about safeguarding dignity.

questions.q: The brevity of the residents' handbook is most directly explained by
opts: Sayid's refusal to permit publication of his methods.
the fact that his practice rested on unspoken judgments he had never articulated.
the residents' inexperience as observers.
an editorial decision by the hospital administration.
questions.why: The final paragraph attributes the handbook's slimness to Sayid's surgical method being "a synthesis of judgments he had not bothered to make explicit even to himself."

10.title: A Posthumous Reading
10.text:
Edith Marlowe published four slim novels between 1962 and 1978 and then, by her own account, stopped writing. She lived another thirty-one years in a small town in Maine, taught middle-school English, and declined every interview request she received. When she died in 2009, the obituary in the regional paper was modest: a paragraph about her teaching, a paragraph about her gardens, a single line that mentioned her books.

The posthumous reception, when it began three years later, was fraught from the outset. A young critic at a literary quarterly had reread the novels and recast Marlowe — in a long, fervent essay — as a major figure whose primacy in mid-century American fiction had been overlooked. The essay was widely shared. Within a year, two of the novels had been reissued. Within three, Marlowe had become the subject of a small but durable academic field, and the watershed seemed to have arrived: a quiet writer, lionized at last.

The lionization, however, has not gone uncontested. A more evenhanded school of criticism has begun to read the novels at moderate distance, neither inflating them nor diminishing them. These critics point out that Marlowe's books are very good but that the recasting of her as a neglected master has tarnished the more interesting question of why she stopped writing at all. The fervent essay, they argue, reads her silence as a blemish to be explained away — a circumstance to be redeemed by belated celebration — rather than as a deliberate choice deserving its own respect.

The synthesis the more careful critics propose is one Marlowe herself might have endorsed, although she yearned during her lifetime for no critical attention whatever. The novels articulate, in a perceptible and disciplined voice, exactly what their author wanted them to say. The thirty-one years of teaching and gardening that followed are not a sad coda; they are the rest of the life. To honor Marlowe, on this reading, is not to resurrect her career. It is to accept the renewal that her own decision to stop writing represented — to let the four books be the four books, and to let her demise, when it came, end a life that had been complete long before its final hour.

questions.q: The passage's central disagreement among critics is over
opts: whether Marlowe's novels are aesthetically successful.
how to interpret Marlowe's decision to stop writing after 1978.
whether her novels should be reissued in academic editions.
the accuracy of her obituary in the regional paper.
questions.why: The third and fourth paragraphs frame the dispute precisely around the meaning of her silence — whether it is a blemish to be explained away or a deliberate choice to be respected.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the position the author seems to favor?
opts: Marlowe's silence should be interpreted as evidence of personal failure.
Marlowe's career should be celebrated through aggressive academic recovery.
Marlowe's silence was a deliberate choice deserving its own respect.
Marlowe's novels are inferior to those of her contemporaries.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph endorses the more careful critics' synthesis, framing Marlowe's silence as part of a complete life rather than a fault to be redeemed.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "the watershed seemed to have arrived" most directly conveys
opts: an unequivocal triumph of belated recognition.
an apparent turning point whose meaning the passage will subsequently complicate.
the moment at which Marlowe's novels first entered print.
the specific date of the critic's first essay.
questions.why: The word "seemed" signals the appearance of a turning point, which the next paragraph immediately complicates by introducing the more evenhanded critics.

11.title: The Cartographer
11.text:
Reuben Aldis had been called a misanthrope so often, by so many people, that he had stopped contesting the description. He was not, in fact, hostile to humanity; he was simply itinerant by disposition, and he had built a career around the salient fact that detailed coastline cartography requires long stretches of solitary fieldwork. He worked under contract for two academic presses and one government agency, and he had, since 1991, walked and surveyed nearly every accessible mile of shoreline in the northeastern Atlantic provinces.

His method was detached and patient. He kept a notebook in which he scribbled subtle observations the satellite imagery could not yet decipher: the way a particular cove silted differently after a winter of unusual ice, the manifest movement of a sandbar that two earlier surveys had missed. He distrusted the rambling speculation of colleagues who built theories from a single visit to a coast. The shoreline, he liked to say, would not be hurried into making sense; it caters to no one's deadline.

What acquaintances mistook for hostility was, on closer inspection, an abiding preference for the salubrious quiet of the field. Reuben was not garrulous, but he was not unkind. He sent placid letters to his sister every Sunday from whatever town his work had brought him to, and he kept up a small correspondence with a retired colleague in Halifax whom he had not seen in person in eleven years. The places he haunted by choice — small inns, quiet libraries, the cafés that catered to the local fishing trade — were a refuge from the kind of professional gathering that, in his view, generated more rambling than insight.

The novel he was rumored, late in his career, to be writing turned out, when his executors examined the manuscript, to be something else: a slow, uncompromising prose record of the coast itself, organized cove by cove, with nothing of the personal in it. It was published last year, two summers after his death. The reviews were valiant attempts to find a story in the book and, fortuitously for the publisher, the absence of one prevailed as the book's most discussed feature. Readers came to it expecting a man's life. They found, instead, a coast — and the man, by his own design, only in the patience of the looking.

questions.q: The passage suggests that Reuben's reputation as a misanthrope is
opts: an accurate description of his deep hostility toward people.
a misreading of a temperament better understood as itinerant solitude.
the result of a single public dispute with a colleague.
a label he actively cultivated to deter visitors.
questions.why: The first and third paragraphs explicitly distinguish his solitude and itinerant disposition from hostility — a misreading rather than the accurate description.

questions.q: The book published after Reuben's death is described as notable for
opts: its dramatic account of his personal relationships.
its absence of personal narrative, which reviewers ultimately found significant.
its argument with the academic presses he had worked for.
its inclusion of unpublished correspondence with his sister.
questions.why: The final paragraph specifies that the absence of a story "prevailed as the book's most discussed feature" — that absence is what reviewers focused on.

questions.q: The contrast in the third paragraph between the placid letters and the absent professional gatherings primarily serves to
opts: establish that Reuben was wealthier than colleagues realized.
show that his preference for quiet was selective rather than indiscriminate.
introduce a disagreement with his sister.
emphasize that he could not write professional papers.
questions.why: The contrast — sustained correspondence on one hand, avoidance of conferences on the other — illustrates that his withdrawal was selective: from rambling gatherings, not from people in general.

11.title: The Pedagogue
11.text:
When the new principal at Hartwell Middle School announced that the language arts curriculum would be downsized to make room for a test-preparation block, the response from the faculty was, in the staff lounge at least, immediate and uncompromising. Mrs. Iris Coyne, the senior English teacher, lambasted the proposal as a stale repetition of every reform she had survived since the inception of her career. The arguments for it, she said, were plausible only to those who had never taught a child to read.

Her position, articulated at the next school-board meeting, was salient and not at all rambling. The general claim that test scores measured something worth optimizing was, she argued, a frivolous one when applied to a population still acquiring fluency. The cornerstone of pedagogy at her grade level had to be the slow work of edifying a reader — building, by subtle increments, the kinds of attention and patience that no test in the district's bank could detect. To downsize that work in the name of measurable gains was a pedagogical move so untenable that it would, within three years, manifest as exactly the regression it had been advertised to prevent.

The board, fraught and divided, censured no one but accepted few of the principal's proposed cuts. The principal, to her credit, did not retaliate. She did not censor the dissenting teachers in their classrooms; she did not augment the pressure on Mrs. Coyne in the small ways that administrators sometimes find at their disposal. She conceded, in a memo three months later, that her original framing had been incomplete, and she invited the faculty to propose what they considered more pedagogically defensible adjustments to the schedule.

The revisions, when they were drafted, were a novel feat of compromise. Mrs. Coyne, who had been the loudest voice of dissent, became one of the most useful members of the redesign committee. The new schedule did not increase the test-preparation block, and it did not pretend to be a panacea. What it did was preserve, as a kind of professional commitment, the principle that the slow work of literacy could not be downsized into a more efficient pedagogy without ceasing to be literacy at all. Mrs. Coyne retired four years later. The schedule, as far as I know, is still in use.

questions.q: Mrs. Coyne's central objection to the principal's original proposal is that it
opts: would burden teachers with additional grading responsibilities.
would mistake measurable test gains for the actual aim of literacy instruction.
would unfairly target experienced senior teachers for dismissal.
would require the school to purchase new testing software.
questions.why: The second paragraph frames her argument: optimizing test scores is frivolous when the real cornerstone is slow literacy work that no test can detect.

questions.q: The principal's behavior after the board meeting is best described as
opts: vindictive, using subtle means to punish dissenting teachers.
indifferent, declining to engage with the faculty further.
responsive, conceding ground and inviting collaboration.
deceptive, pretending compromise while implementing cuts.
questions.why: The third paragraph specifies she did not retaliate, conceded incompleteness, and invited the faculty to propose alternatives — responsive rather than vindictive.

questions.q: The closing paragraph functions in the passage primarily to
opts: predict that the new schedule will eventually be reversed.
describe how a successful resolution preserved a principle without claiming a final solution.
criticize Mrs. Coyne for retiring at an inopportune moment.
reveal that the principal was eventually fired.
questions.why: The closing paragraph notes the schedule "did not pretend to be a panacea" but preserved the underlying principle — a description of a partial, principled resolution.

11.title: The Bridge
11.text:
When the engineers began work on the new river crossing in 1932, the project was a modest one. The bridge was to span less than four hundred feet at a salient narrowing of the river, and the design — a steel truss anchored on two stone piers — was, in the language of the period, the cornerstone of competent provincial engineering. The state had budgeted for a two-year construction. The chief engineer, a man named Whittaker, had agreed.

By the third year, the budget had ballooned, and the timetable had become, by any plausible measure, untenable. The piers were the trouble. The riverbed at the chosen narrowing was deeper than the inception surveys had suggested; the bedrock was fissured in patterns the geologists had not anticipated. Workers had been petrified, on at least two occasions, by the sudden displacement of caissons in unexpected currents. The local press, which had at first lionized the project, began to speculate openly about the perilous management of the work.

Whittaker did not dissemble. In a letter to the state engineering office that survives in the regional archive, he described the situation in uncompromising terms. The original design was no longer viable. The piers would have to be redesigned to anchor at a different depth, and the truss redrawn to augment the load-bearing capacity over a longer effective span. The valiant adjustment, he argued, was not to abandon the bridge but to acknowledge that the inception estimates had been wrong and to rebuild from a more inclusive understanding of the site. He requested, in the same letter, that the budget be increased by forty percent.

The state granted the request, with conditions. The bridge opened in 1937, two years after the original deadline, and it has been in continuous service for eighty-eight years. The subtle revision Whittaker negotiated has prevailed against the river through nine recorded floods, including one in 1989 that destroyed two adjacent bridges built later under more confident assumptions. What the project demonstrates, on the abiding reading of engineering historians, is not the heroism of any single decision but the discipline of a chief engineer who would not let an early estimate become a constraint on the truth of the site. The bridge stands. The original budget does not.

questions.q: The central virtue the passage attributes to Whittaker is
opts: his ability to deliver projects under their original budget.
his willingness to revise estimates rather than defend them against contrary evidence.
his charisma in negotiating with the state engineering office.
his reliance on the inception surveys throughout the project.
questions.why: The third and fourth paragraphs emphasize his refusal to dissemble and his insistence that the inception estimates had been wrong — a willingness to revise rather than defend.

questions.q: The reference to the 1989 flood functions in the passage primarily to
opts: explain why the original budget had to be increased.
demonstrate that even the revised bridge was eventually destroyed.
support the claim that the revised design has held up better than later, more confident ones.
introduce a new generation of engineers.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph contrasts the bridge's survival with the destruction of "two adjacent bridges built later under more confident assumptions" — supporting the claim about the value of revised, humble design.

questions.q: In context, the closing line — "The bridge stands. The original budget does not" — most directly emphasizes
opts: a contrast between durable engineering judgment and an obsolete financial estimate.
the ongoing financial costs of maintaining old infrastructure.
a rebuke of Whittaker for going over budget.
the historical accuracy of all original cost projections.
questions.why: The closing line opposes the persistence of the bridge to the obsolescence of the original budget — making the budget, not the engineering, the disposable thing.

11.title: Counterintuitive
11.text:
The economist's central finding, when she presented it at the conference, struck most of the audience as counterintuitive. She had been studying the effect of small unconditional cash transfers on rural households, and her data suggested that recipients did not, as the prevailing speculation had assumed, spend the funds primarily on consumption. They saved them, in modest amounts, and they used the savings to make small but salient investments — a sewing machine, a goat, a year of school fees — that augmented household income within twenty-four months.

The finding was not, on inspection, novel. Earlier work in three other countries had suggested something similar. What was novel was the rigor of the new study and the size of the effect, which was substantially larger than even the most optimistic of the previous estimates. Her presentation was uncompromising in its presentation of the methodology, detached in its discussion of the data, and moderate in its general claims about implications. She did not predicate any policy recommendation on the findings. She merely showed what the data manifested.

The response from the audience was, by the standards of an academic conference, fraught. Several senior economists lambasted the work for what they called rambling extrapolation; others objected on theoretical grounds that the result, however well-documented, was untenable as a general matter of household economics. A junior economist, whose own work had been built on the older speculation, attempted to censure the methodology by raising a procedural concern that turned out, on subsequent inspection, to be plausible only at first hearing.

The author did not respond combatively. She acknowledged each objection, deciphered the most substantive ones in writing in the months that followed, and revised her paper on the points where the criticism had been correct. Where it had not been correct, she let the data, in subsequent replications, prevail. Two years later, the central finding has been replicated in four more contexts, and the abiding reception of the original paper has shifted from skepticism to a fortuitous kind of consensus — fortuitous because, as she remarked at a later conference, no one had set out to overturn an existing assumption. The data had simply, on its own subtle schedule, asked a question the existing assumption could not answer.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the principal reason the original audience reacted with hostility was that
opts: the methodology was demonstrably flawed.
the result threatened a body of prevailing assumptions about household behavior.
the author had personally insulted senior economists in attendance.
the data had been collected illegally.
questions.why: The third paragraph attributes objections to theoretical grounds and to the threat the result posed to prior speculation, particularly for those whose work had been built on it.

questions.q: The author's response to the criticism is best characterized as
opts: defiant refusal to engage with any objections.
selective acknowledgment, revising where critics were correct and letting the data answer where they were not.
complete capitulation to the senior economists' demands.
withdrawal of the paper from publication.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph specifies that she revised on points where criticism was correct and let replication prevail where it was not — a selective, evidence-based engagement.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "a fortuitous kind of consensus" most nearly conveys that the agreement was
opts: manufactured through political pressure on dissenting economists.
the unintended result of accumulated evidence rather than a coordinated effort.
limited to the small group of replicators in four countries.
based on a misunderstanding of the original paper.
questions.why: The closing sentences specify that no one set out to overturn the assumption — the consensus emerged from the data "on its own subtle schedule," hence fortuitous rather than orchestrated.

11.title: The Debate Club
11.text:
When I joined the university debate club at the inception of my second year, I was not, by any honest accounting, a neophyte. I had argued for sport since I was fourteen. But the club was a new kind of room, and within a week I understood that what I had taken for skill was, in this company, the boisterous garrulity of a tyro who had never been seriously contradicted.

The club's culture was uncompromising and not, in the early sessions, kind. The captain, a soft-spoken third-year named Priya, was famously blunt in her feedback. "You waffled," she told me after my first practice round, in front of the assembled members. "Twice. Once at the top, once on rebuttal. The salient claim was the third one, and you buried it." I had been ebullient about the round. I left it considerably less so.

What the club taught, over the following months, was a subtle discipline that no formal coaching had prepared me for. A frivolous flourish — a clever phrase, a witty aside — could not be permitted to augment a weak argument; it could only manifest the weakness more clearly to a careful judge. A plausible objection, however quietly raised, had to be answered on its merits and not waved off. The general principle was that a debater's job was to be useful to the audience's thinking, not impressive to its momentary attention. I faltered, in the early weeks, to internalize this. By December I had stopped reaching, instinctively, for the easy effect.

The valiant feat, by Priya's standards, was not winning. She censured boastfulness about wins as much as she censured sloppy argument. The feat was the round in which a debater had argued so cleanly that the audience could leave with a clearer view of the question than they had brought to the room. I do not remember which of my rounds, exactly, qualified as such; I do remember the moderate, almost grudging nod Priya gave me at the end of the spring semester, which I have prized more, since, than any tournament result. The abiding lesson of the club was that argument was not performance. It was service. Whatever has prevailed in my thinking from those years, that lesson is the one I have most often had to relearn.

questions.q: The narrator's central realization upon joining the club was that
opts: his earlier debate experience had been wasted.
what he had thought of as skill was, in serious company, the noise of a beginner.
the club's expectations were unreasonably harsh.
Priya had personal grievances against new members.
questions.why: The first paragraph explicitly redescribes his prior skill as "the boisterous garrulity of a tyro" once measured against the club's standards.

questions.q: Priya's standard for a successful round is best described as
opts: winning a tournament against strong opposition.
leaving the audience with a clearer view of the question than they had at the start.
making the most witty and memorable rhetorical statements.
ensuring no factual error appears in the speech.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph names her standard directly: a round in which the audience leaves with a clearer view of the question — service rather than victory.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "a frivolous flourish... could only manifest the weakness more clearly" implies that
opts: rhetorical decoration tends to expose, rather than conceal, a weak underlying argument.
humor is forbidden in formal debate.
audiences cannot tell the difference between strong and weak arguments.
rhetorical skill is itself a kind of weakness.
questions.why: The sentence specifically frames flourish as making weakness more visible to a careful judge — exposing rather than concealing the argument's flaws.

12.title: The Acidic Sea
12.text:
The ocean is becoming more acidic, and the change is, by any sober measure, marked. When Dr. Lina Faro began to scrutinize the seawater off the Oregon coast in 2004, the shift was almost indiscernible to anyone but a chemist with a good pH meter. By the time she resurfaced a decade later with a longer dataset, the numbers had become a sobering compendium of small but elemental losses.

The chemistry, in outline, is not in dispute. Carbon dioxide dissolved into seawater forms carbonic acid; the more we emit, the more acidic the surface ocean becomes. What forebodes a real problem is the rate. Past acidification events, recorded in the fossil record of aboriginal coral reefs, unfolded over tens of thousands of years. The current shift has been hastened into the span of a single century. Putative thresholds for shell-building organisms — the small, almost indiscernible larvae of oysters, the pteropods that mimic translucent butterflies under a microscope — are being crossed already.

Dr. Faro is careful not to traffic in the spectacular. Her grant reports avoid the word "crisis" the way her colleagues' do not. Yet she is unwilling to curtail the implications of her findings to placate a hospitable funder. The acidification, she says, will not be a sudden event one can preempt with a single piece of legislation. It will be a slow narrowing of the conditions in which certain species can persist — a fluctuating squeeze rather than a single blow. Pathogen outbreaks among already-stressed shellfish populations have begun to proliferate in ways that suggest the squeeze is well under way.

What she finds difficult, in lectures, is the public's appetite for a single villain. There is no villain. There is only the ascendant fact of a chemistry that no one, individually, intended. The fishermen who have been her partners since the first sampling year have, by now, domesticated the bad news into a workable plan; their hatcheries buffer their seed water and tackle each season with adjusted expectations. It is, she tells her students, the unglamorous shape of adaptation. The cliff is not a cliff. The cliff is a long downhill road one can still steer on, if one looks.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?
opts: Past acidification events were more severe than the current one.
Ocean acidification will be sudden and can be preempted by single laws.
Acidification poses a real threat chiefly because of its rate, not its magnitude alone.
Pteropods are the only species threatened by acidification.
questions.why: The second paragraph foregrounds the rate ("hastened into the span of a single century") as what distinguishes the current shift from prior natural events.

questions.q: Dr. Faro's reluctance to use the word "crisis" most directly serves to
opts: show that she does not believe the data are reliable.
establish her credibility as someone whose alarm is not rhetorical.
indicate that she is concealing findings from her funders.
suggest she has lost interest in the work.
questions.why: The third paragraph contrasts her avoidance of "crisis" with her unwillingness to curtail the implications, framing her as principled rather than alarmist.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the image of "a long downhill road one can still steer on" most directly conveys
opts: that the problem will solve itself without intervention.
that adaptation is impossible without a single villain.
that the situation is bad but still navigable through deliberate adjustment.
that fishermen should abandon hatcheries entirely.
questions.why: The image follows the description of fishermen adjusting their hatcheries and expectations — adaptation through deliberate steering, not solved nor hopeless.

12.title: The Supercilious Dealer
12.text:
Reginald Hayle had run a small but reputable gallery on Cork Street for thirty-one years, and had earned, in that time, a reputation for being supercilious that no friend of his had ever quite managed to extenuate. He was officious to the wrong people and unfailingly decorous to the right ones. He patronized younger dealers with an assuming, almost perfidious warmth that vanished the moment a sale was secured. The few collectors who had been bold enough to rail against his manner had found, soon enough, that their own access to certain estates had grown indolent and obscure.

My first encounter with him was in 1998, when I had been sent, presumptuously, to scrutinize a small Bonnard he had claimed to be selling on behalf of a discreet European family. The provenance documents were anodyne in tone and almost too clean. Reginald watched me read them with the marked patience of a man who had long ago stopped being discomfited by the suspicions of others. "You will find," he said, in a voice that managed to be both circumspect and faintly bored, "that the chimera of forgery is the favorite hobby of those who cannot afford the real thing."

I did not, in the end, recommend the painting. The bias against Reginald in my own training had been thorough, and there were small details — a hideous repainted corner, a stretcher older than its canvas — that no extenuation he offered seemed quite tenable. He did not assail me when I declined. He simply smiled, said something plebeian about my employer, and moved the Bonnard to a less scrupulous house, where it sold within the month.

What I learned from him, perversely, was less about authentication than about the social architecture of a market that runs on trust nobody can quite define. Reginald was not, on any measurable scale, a fraud. He was, instead, a man who had calibrated his manner so precisely to the room that the room seldom noticed it. The decorous lunches, the supercilious nods to junior staff, the officious telephone manner with widows — these were not accidents of temperament. They were the machinery by which a certain kind of business was, and is, conducted. I have not gone back to Cork Street since his retirement. I doubt the architecture has changed.

questions.q: The narrator's view of Reginald by the end of the passage is best described as
opts: convinced that he was an outright forger.
persuaded that his manner was the deliberate machinery of his trade.
regretful that he was driven from the gallery world.
indifferent to whether his methods were legitimate.
questions.why: The final paragraph explicitly calls his manner "the machinery by which a certain kind of business was, and is, conducted" — calibrated, not accidental.

questions.q: Reginald's remark that "the chimera of forgery is the favorite hobby of those who cannot afford the real thing" most directly functions as
opts: an admission that the painting is fake.
an attempt to discomfit the narrator by reframing suspicion as envy.
a sincere reflection on the art market's history.
a request that the narrator examine the canvas more carefully.
questions.why: The remark recasts the narrator's scrutiny as the petty hobby of those who cannot buy — a maneuver designed to discomfit, not to inform.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, the word "tenable" most nearly means
opts: expensive to maintain.
able to be defended or sustained as plausible.
willing to be accepted by buyers.
consistent with the gallery's pricing policy.
questions.why: The narrator decides Reginald's extenuations cannot stand against the physical evidence — "tenable" here means able to be defensibly maintained.

12.title: Terminology
12.text:
Court interpreters are paid, in the official terminology of the Ministry of Justice, to render the proceedings "into and from the relevant language with fidelity." They are not paid, the contract continues, to extenuate, to preempt, or to misrepresent. In practice, no interpreter who has worked more than a year takes the contract's confidence at face value. A judge's colloquial aside, a witness's tearful digression, a hardliner's prepared speech disguised as testimony — each carries its own small mishap, and the interpreter is the only person in the room obliged to recollect what was actually said before deciding how to render it.

My own induction was an afternoon of disinformation cases at the magistrate's court in 2012. I had been told, presumptuously by a colleague whose advice I now scrutinize more carefully, that the sessions would be "largely formulaic." The first witness's testimony was nothing of the sort. He spoke a dialect that my training had only glanced at, and his account of a fraudulent tender involved technical terminology in three industries at once. I was circumspect about adjourning to consult my dictionary; the judge looked liable to be officious about delay. When I finally asked, the judge, to my surprise, was decisive and patient in equal measure. "Take your time," she said. "This is what the room is for."

What I did not yet understand was that the indispensable virtue of the interpreter, on a given day, is not speed. It is the willingness to be slow when slowness is what fidelity requires. A hasty rendering of a hardliner's careful evasions can demoralize a witness's defense before counsel has noticed anything has gone wrong. A factious courtroom — and they were, in those years, often factious — will seize on any mishap to argue that the interpretation is itself a putative form of misrepresentation. The interpreter who hurries to seem competent is, in a real sense, complicit in that misreading.

I think of that judge often, especially when I train new interpreters. The lesson she gave was so plainly offered that I almost missed it. The room exists for the speaker to be heard, and for the hearer to understand. Anything that rushes either is, in the small and unglamorous way that justice is administered, a tiny dereliction. We are not paid to be quick. We are paid to be exactly right.

questions.q: The passage's primary purpose is to
opts: argue that court interpreters should be paid more than they currently are.
explain why interpreters' professional virtue depends on a willingness to be slow when fidelity demands it.
criticize judges who rush proceedings to clear their dockets.
describe the technical training required of court interpreters.
questions.why: The third paragraph explicitly identifies "the willingness to be slow when slowness is what fidelity requires" as the indispensable virtue — the central claim of the piece.

questions.q: The judge's response to the narrator's request to consult a dictionary functions in the passage primarily to
opts: show that she had been bored by the proceedings.
model the principle the narrator will later articulate.
demonstrate the judge's lack of legal training.
introduce a personal friendship that develops between the two.
questions.why: The judge's "This is what the room is for" enacts, before the narrator names it, the principle that fidelity outranks speed.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "a tiny dereliction" in the final paragraph refers to
opts: an interpreter's deliberate refusal to translate a passage.
a judge's failure to learn a foreign language.
any rushing that compromises either being heard or being understood.
the structural underfunding of the courts.
questions.why: The phrase comes immediately after "Anything that rushes either is" — i.e., any rushing that compromises hearing or understanding.

12.title: The Genealogist
12.text:
My grandmother's compendium of family papers had sat, untouched and indiscernible from the surrounding clutter, on the top shelf of a hall closet for the better part of forty years. It was given to me in the summer after her funeral, and I spent the autumn assembling its contents on my dining-room table, trying to scrutinize each fragment without too quickly assuming what it was. There were marriage certificates in three languages, a christening robe whose wearer no one could now recollect, and a strange envelope of photographs whose putative subjects had been, in family lore, more or less interchangeable.

What I had set out to do was, in the genealogist's tame phrase, "verify the line." What I had not foreseen was the marked discomfort of that work. Several of the more circumspect facts I had grown up with did not survive contact with the documents. A great-uncle whose military service had been the family's quiet pride had, on inspection, deserted twice. A pagan wedding in a Lithuanian village in 1893, dismissed by my mother as disinformation passed down by a sentimental aunt, turned out to be tenable on the evidence of three separate parish records. To renounce the family stories I had inherited was not what I had wanted. To rehash them in the polished form they had taken in childhood was no longer possible.

My father, when I told him, was reflective in a way I had not expected. He did not extenuate the discrepancies; he did not insist that the documents had to be misread. He simply observed that every family was, in the end, a compendium of stories that had been edited as much for survival as for truth. "Your grandmother knew where the bodies were," he said, and laughed at his own phrase. "What she did not know — what no one knows about their own family — is which versions of those bodies were going to be displaced by the next generation's appetite for a clean narrative."

I have not finished the project. Two of the photographs still lack a confirmed whereabouts in the family tree, and a fourth language has surfaced in a folded letter I cannot yet read. But the work has shifted in my hands. I no longer think of myself as the family's auditor. I think of myself, on a sober day, as one of its custodians: someone whose task is not to predetermine which version of the past survives but to make sure no version is quietly thrown away.

questions.q: The narrator's understanding of her project shifts most clearly from
opts: auditing the family's stories to preserving every available version of them.
preserving stories to discarding ones she finds inconvenient.
writing a memoir to producing an academic paper.
trusting her grandmother to distrusting all family lore.
questions.why: The closing paragraph explicitly contrasts "the family's auditor" with "one of its custodians," whose job is to keep versions from being discarded.

questions.q: The father's remark about "which versions of those bodies were going to be displaced" most directly suggests that family stories are
opts: always intentionally fabricated by the older generation.
subject to gradual revision shaped by what later generations need to hear.
more reliable than written documents.
uniquely vulnerable to legal challenges.
questions.why: The father frames every family as a compendium edited for survival, with later generations' "appetite for a clean narrative" doing the editing — gradual revision, not deliberate fabrication.

questions.q: The discovery about the great-uncle and the Lithuanian wedding is included primarily to
opts: demonstrate the narrator's superior research skills.
concretize the discomfort of finding that received family stories do not survive scrutiny.
argue that pagan weddings should be more widely recognized.
explain why the great-uncle was eventually pardoned.
questions.why: Both examples are introduced to illustrate "the marked discomfort" of the work — they ground the abstract claim in concrete instances.

12.title: An Amateur Lexicographer
12.text:
Mr. Galt was the librarian of a small parish in County Mayo, and the most pertinacious amateur lexicographer I have ever known. His salary was exiguous; his office, a converted vestry, was always impecunious in the matter of paper. He was not jealous of professional dictionary-makers in the cities, although he might reasonably have been; the cupidity of academic publishing did not appear to interest him in any visible way. He simply tinkered, year after year, at a compendium of local Irish-English usages that he had begun, ingenuously, in his early thirties.

I met him in his sixty-fourth year, when I had been sent — by a university editor with more acumen than budget — to assess the work for possible publication. The card index alone filled three filing cabinets. Each entry had been scrutinized at least twice in his neat, slightly officious handwriting; entries he was uncertain of were marked with a small circumspect star and a date for re-examination. The collection was not spectacular in the way the magazines like their stories to be. It was, instead, a quiet paragon of versatile, rote-defeating attention to a vocabulary that was already in its waning years.

What struck me, on the first day, was how indolent the room felt despite the obvious labor it housed. Mr. Galt did not bore his visitors with the scope of his enterprise. He poured tea. He asked, with the ascendant gentleness of a man who had long ago made peace with his obscurity, what I made of the gloss on a particular Donegal verb. When I admitted I had never heard of it, he did not patronize me; he simply rehashed, with a small smile, the three regional sources he had triangulated.

The compendium reached, in his eighty-first year, what I would call its apogee. It was published, eventually, by a small university press in a print run small enough to embarrass the academic world. Mr. Galt himself did not live to see its second edition. What survives, on my own shelf, is a copy he inscribed in his last winter — "For the editor who came up the long road," it reads — and the much larger memory of a man who had taken a kind of work that no one had asked him to do and pursued it with a private devotion that put the rest of us, scribblers and tinkerers as we are, to a useful and lasting shame.

questions.q: The author's primary purpose in describing Mr. Galt is to
opts: argue that amateur lexicographers should be paid as well as professionals.
honor a quiet, sustained form of intellectual devotion that institutions tend to overlook.
criticize academic publishing for its slow timelines.
compare Irish-English to other regional dialects.
questions.why: The closing paragraph reframes Mr. Galt's small print run and decades of unsponsored labor as "a useful and lasting shame" to professional scribblers — honoring his unglamorous devotion.

questions.q: The narrator's description of Mr. Galt as not "jealous" of professional dictionary-makers most directly serves to
opts: imply that he secretly resented their salaries.
establish that his motivation was not professional rivalry but private interest.
indicate that he had once tried and failed to obtain a university post.
suggest that he was unaware of academic dictionaries.
questions.why: The contrast preempts the obvious motive (envy of better-funded peers) and clears space for the alternative the passage develops: a private, non-rivalrous devotion.

questions.q: In context, the phrase "the room felt indolent" in the third paragraph most nearly means that the room
opts: was filled with people who were not working.
had an unhurried, restful atmosphere despite the labor it contained.
was poorly maintained and dusty.
had been abandoned for long stretches of the year.
questions.why: The sentence specifies "despite the obvious labor it housed," so "indolent" here describes the room's unhurried atmosphere, not actual idleness.

13.title: The Glossy Editor
13.text:
Vera Mendoza had edited the glossy for eleven years, and in that time she had refused, almost as a point of professional honor, to relinquish the magazine's stickler standards to the more lenient norms of the digital age. The print issue still appeared on schedule, lavish and thick, on the first Thursday of each month. Its cover stories were exorbitant in their reporting budgets and caustic in their conclusions; her finesse with reluctant subjects had become a small industry secret.

What her detractors said about her was not, on its merits, disingenuous. She was self-aggrandizing in interviews. She could be peremptory with junior staff, particularly those who arrived with the halfhearted preparation that the open-plan culture of newer magazines had begun to encourage. Her amicable lunches with publishers were, more often than not, the prelude to a piece that would savage one of their competitors. To imagine her as the egalitarian colleague the trade press sometimes painted was, in any case, a presumptuous reading of the woman herself.

What the same detractors missed was that the standards she enforced were not personal vanity. They were, in her own private terminology, the cement that kept the title from being supplanted by the indulgent stream of content that had eroded every glossy around her. "A magazine," she had told me once, in a hectic afternoon between two closes, "is not a feed. It is a discrete object that arrives once a month and asks the reader to introspect for ninety minutes. Once you forget that, you are no longer editing a magazine. You are managing a website that happens to print."

When she finally retired, the obituaries — for that is what the trade pieces amounted to — were predictably lavish in praise and discreet about her temper. The successor she chose was an introspective former staff writer who had spent a decade quietly disagreeing with her, and to whom she had, surprisingly, relinquished a share of editorial authority in her last year. In the more mundane reckoning of the industry, the magazine was no longer ascendant. In the harder reckoning of what one actually had on Thursday morning, it was, for one more decade at least, a glossy that meant something. Vera, characteristically, did not stay to see how long the meaning lasted.

questions.q: The author's view of Vera is best described as
opts: uncritically admiring of her style and her temperament.
respectful of her standards while acknowledging the flaws her detractors named.
convinced that she destroyed the magazine through her temper.
indifferent to her tenure at the magazine.
questions.why: The second paragraph concedes the detractors' points were not disingenuous; the third defends her standards as substantive — a respect-with-acknowledged-flaws posture, not pure praise.

questions.q: Vera's distinction between a magazine and a feed primarily functions to
opts: ridicule her younger colleagues for their reading habits.
articulate the editorial principle her standards were meant to defend.
explain why the magazine's circulation had risen.
concede that print magazines have no future.
questions.why: The distinction ("a discrete object" vs. "a feed") is the principle her stickler standards were meant to protect — the philosophical core of her editing.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the phrase "the harder reckoning" most nearly refers to
opts: a stricter financial accounting of the magazine's losses.
an evaluation based on the actual quality of what readers received, not on industry trends.
a confidential review by the magazine's owners.
the magazine's coverage of difficult news topics.
questions.why: The contrast with "the more mundane reckoning of the industry" (trends, ascendancy) makes "the harder reckoning" the one based on what readers actually got Thursday morning.

13.title: The Chronicle of the Flood
13.text:
The 1361 flood of the Yellow River was, by the chronicle of the Yuan official Tao Zongyi, presaged for almost a year before it came. The summer rains of 1360 had been ominous in volume and in timing; the dykes upriver, which had been cemented haphazardly during a previous administration, began to show incipient cracks that no halfhearted local repair could retrieve. Tao's own dispatches to the capital, which he wrote with a secular and unsentimental hand, are an early model of what historians today call risk reportage. They are also, by his own admission, the chronicle of an inexorable disaster he could not premeditate his way around.

The cataclysm, when it arrived in the seventh month, displaced an estimated three hundred thousand people. Whole villages were eroded into the silt within a single afternoon. What is striking about Tao's account is not its scale — many earlier flood records had given comparable figures — but its discrete attention to administrative failure. The grain stores that had been siphoned by corrupt officials in the previous decade left the relief effort without the buffer it was supposed to have. The dyke repair budget, on paper feasible, had been muddled across three ministries until no one was responsible for any single segment. The flood, akin to many such events in Chinese history, was not the chronicle of nature alone. It was the chronicle of a state whose capacity to respond had been hollowed out long before the rain.

Later scholars have crabbed at Tao's analysis on technical grounds. His river hydraulics are simplistic; his population estimates have been snagged on the documentary record more than once. None of this, however, has displaced the central thrust of his reporting, which was that a cataclysm spurred by weather had been made survivable, or unsurvivable, by decades of prior choices.

To introspect on the chronicle today, in a century with its own ominous rivers, is to be reminded that the genre has always done a particular kind of work. The chronicler does not predict. The chronicler watches what was already in motion, and writes it down with care, so that the next administration cannot easily endanger its own people by claiming, when the water rises, that no one had seen it coming.

questions.q: The passage's central argument about Tao Zongyi's chronicle is that it
opts: exaggerated the scale of the 1361 flood for political reasons.
treated the disaster primarily as a meteorological event.
located the cause of the cataclysm in administrative decisions made long before the flood.
was the first scientific account of river hydraulics in Chinese history.
questions.why: The second and third paragraphs repeatedly emphasize Tao's discrete attention to administrative failure and "decades of prior choices," not weather alone.

questions.q: The author's response to later scholars' technical criticisms of Tao is best described as
opts: dismissive of the criticisms as politically motivated.
willing to grant the technical points while preserving the argument's core.
uncertain whether the criticisms can be answered at all.
sympathetic with the scholars' attempt to discredit Tao entirely.
questions.why: The third paragraph concedes that scholars have valid technical complaints ("None of this, however...") but insists the central thrust survives — a granting-with-preservation posture.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the author argues that the chronicler's work is to
opts: predict future disasters before they occur.
record what is already in motion so that future officials cannot deny prior warning.
assign blame to specific corrupt officials by name.
produce hydraulic data for the next administration.
